item.title: Hackers Hijack Five OVHcloud CLI Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware
item.description:
A hijacked contributor account swapped malware into five OVHcloud CLI releases for 94 minutes on October 19, targeting secrets on any machine that ran the poisoned binary during that window.
Key findings:
- The attacker replaced six files on v0.15.0 and the same files on v0.11.0 through v0.14.0: macOS x86_64 and arm64, Linux x86_64 and arm64, Windows x86_64, and checksums.txt. The checksums were updated to match the malicious builds, so naive hash checks against the published sums would have passed. The exposure window ran from 12:47 to 14:21 UTC. Linux i386, Windows i386, Windows arm64, and WebAssembly builds were untouched. Homebrew and go install paths were not affected: Homebrew's cask retained the original SHA-256 and would have failed rather than installed the swapped file.
- A customer's CI job caught the swap because it pinned the Linux arm64 SHA-256 and began failing. The only published hash of a swapped archive is that Linux arm64 file: swapped SHA-256 3833daffcaaaab27e4e0e0833240ffcb1df8df648f4ec0bc4a75c176e28933cb, original 5c2beb56e6d83a4b426565a1557791ef759316abcc4effb38dd627c90aeb80e0. No copy of the swapped binary was preserved for analysis, so what it reads or where it sends data remains unknown publicly.
- Three forensic markers separate the bad build from a genuine release, all readable without executing the binary using go version -m. First, the module version string is v0.15.1-0.20261013083505-5ead8ef9b43d+dirty, a pseudo-version from an untagged October 13 commit. Second, the recorded commit is 5ead8ef, not 760fd72, which the v0.15.0 tag actually points to. Third, a -ldflags="-s -w" line is present. OVHcloud's pipeline omits that flag, so genuine releases show no -ldflags line. The +dirty marker alone does not identify the malicious build: the clean v0.16.0 also carries v0.16.0+dirty.
- OpenSourceMalware links the hijacked contributor account to GlassWorm, a campaign that encodes loader stages in invisible Unicode characters and fetches next-stage instructions from the memo field of a Solana wallet's transactions. Four of the account's personal repositories were force-pushed in March with a loader tied to GlassWorm's ForceMemo campaign, which force-pushed malware into hundreds of Python repositories using stolen GitHub tokens. The wallet in that loader matches the one named in ForceMemo. The link between the March activity and the October CLI swap is attributed as an inference based on the shared account, not confirmed code overlap.
- The root cause was GitHub's release immutability setting being disabled on the repository. Anyone with write access to a repo can silently delete and replace release assets with the same filename, and the download URL does not change. GitHub made release immutability generally available in October 2025. OVHcloud had not enabled it; it has now. The release pipeline never ran during the swap: no workflow execution appears between October 16 and the v0.16.0 tag push, confirming the attacker uploaded directly through GitHub's release API using the contributor's credentials.
Practitioner takeaway: if your environment ran the OVHcloud CLI install script or upgrade command between 12:47 and 14:21 UTC on October 19, or pulled any of v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 from a GitHub release page during that window on macOS or Linux x86_64/arm64 or Windows x86_64, treat the machine as compromised. Run go version -m against any copy of the binary you retained without executing it and check the three markers above. Rotate every secret readable from that machine, including ~/.ovh.conf and environment variables, from a separate clean host before removing the binary. Verify v0.16.0 with gh release verify-asset before deploying it. For CI pipelines more broadly: pin SHA-256 hashes of release assets by commit, never by the published checksums file from the same release, and enable GitHub release immutability on any repository that ships binaries. IOCs and timeline details are in OpenSourceMalware's report.

item.title: AOMEI Backupper servers hijacked for minutes at a time to push backdoor
item.description:
AOMEI Backupper supply chain attack: unknown actor hijacked vendor update servers in sub-10-minute windows between May and July 2026 to push a backdoor, hitting IT services, telecom, and higher education across at least 12 countries.
Key details:
- Google tracks the threat actor as UNC7017 with no current country attribution. Confirmed victims span Australia 🇦🇺, Brazil 🇧🇷, India 🇮🇳, Pakistan 🇵🇰, Portugal 🇵🇹, Singapore 🇸🇬, South Africa 🇿🇦, Spain 🇪🇸, Switzerland 🇨🇭, Türkiye, and the United States 🇺🇸, across IT services, telecommunications, and higher education. Victimology was opportunistic, so actual exposure is likely broader than confirmed cases.
- The attack manipulated two AOMEI-hosted config files during confirmed windows on May 28, July 16, and July 20. The file down_html.ini was altered to redirect the software's update mechanism to attacker-controlled download locations with a matching checksum, bypassing the application's own validation. The file Notifycfg.ini was set to silently open an invisible browser window that launched the CROSSROAD dropper. Affected versions start at AOMEI Backupper 8.3.0. AOMEI AnyViewer, which shares the same update mechanism, was also targeted.
- CROSSROAD performed geofencing and sandbox checks: it stopped execution if the host was located in China 🇨🇳, if location could not be determined, or if certain security products were detected. On systems that passed, it installed legitimate Radmin Server alongside the SHINYROAD backdoor and created a scheduled task to execute the backdoor every three hours, then deleted itself to reduce post-infection footprint.
- In the July 20 window, attackers used the Notifycfg.ini pop-up channel to force machines to authenticate against an attacker-controlled WebDAV server, capturing NetNTLMv2 password hashes. This required no malicious code to execute on the endpoint, meaning machines where the dropper was blocked may still have leaked credentials. The full method of initial access to AOMEI's own infrastructure has not been disclosed.
- The attack was first detected by ManageEngine's endpoint software on May 28 when it logged AOMEI Backupper silently installing Radmin on two customer machines in separate countries. Both environments were running in audit mode, so activity was logged but not blocked. The content arrived over HTTPS from AOMEI-owned hostnames through the application's own extraction sequence, ruling out in-transit tampering and confirming server-side compromise.
Practitioner takeaway: Any organization running AOMEI Backupper 8.3.0 or later, or AOMEI AnyViewer, should treat the three confirmed windows (May 28, July 16, July 20, 2026) as potential exposure events. Hunt for Radmin Server installations originating from the AOMEI process, scheduled tasks with a three-hour trigger tied to an unfamiliar executable, and outbound WebDAV authentication events that could indicate hash capture. Check for NetNTLMv2 hash exposure in network logs even on machines where no dropper ran. IOCs are published by ManageEngine and GTIG: pull them and run them across endpoint telemetry, EDR process trees, and scheduled task inventories before assuming a clean bill of health.

item.title: Operation FlashHole: Lazarus breaks security, defies control
item.description:
Lazarus Group's Operation FlashHole targets South Korean 🇰🇷 firms via mandatory financial security software, deploying a fully in-memory malware chain with post-quantum cryptography and GitHub as C2.
Key findings:
- The initial vector abuses CrossWeb EX (INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe), a financial security solution mandatory for South Korean 🇰🇷 online banking and government sites, mirroring Operation SyncHole's abuse of the related Cross EX product. Victims were lured via spearphishing to AI-generated portfolio and resume sites hosted on GitHub Pages, which loaded malicious JavaScript from javadevhouse[.]co[.]kr and pythonapischool[.]com. The legitimate binary fsquirt.exe was injected with shellcode under the CrossWeb EX process, and the entire initial compromise chain ran exclusively in memory. At least three organizations across software, construction, and wired communication equipment manufacturing were confirmed affected, with campaign prep traced to July 2025.
- The malware chain is modular and deeply layered: TechHub (also known as CLOUDBURST and NickelLoader) uses GitHub Personal Access Tokens to communicate via private repositories, staging handshakes through GitHub Issues with a custom RSA-plus-XOR key exchange. TouchHub installs persistence by copying printfilterpipelinesvc.exe to C:\Windows\System32\RasConv\ImeBroker.exe, registering it as a service with a name derived from legitimate netsvcs entries, and side-loading TouchShift as mscoree.dll in the same directory. MAC timestamps are synchronized to C:\Windows\System32\drivers\monitor.sys to hinder timeline analysis. Cubridge (also known as SIDESHOW, LightlessCan) orchestrates post-compromise activity from C2 servers including hxxps://cubedesign[.]co[.]kr/news and hxxps://fp-news[.]co[.]kr/shop/cart using randomized URL paths that mimic news article structures.
- LPEClient, the one malware carried over from Operation SyncHole, received a significant operational overhaul. It no longer holds its own C2 address; instead it communicates via a shared buffer through ClientHub, a newly identified malware assessed with medium-high confidence to be an advanced CookiePlus variant. LPEClient now reads C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS[.]DATA directly to enumerate antivirus products rather than using WQL queries, and queries kernel mitigation states including Kernel VA Shadow and Shadow Stack (CET). Most critically, it implements ML-KEM-1024 (CRYSTALS-Kyber, a NIST post-quantum standard) for key encapsulation and Threefish-256 for payload decryption, making intercepted C2 traffic effectively future-proof against classical decryption.
- Cubridge deploys an action module (ActionModule.dll via AppinfoView export) and a function module (FunctionModule.dll via PresentationFontConfig export) covering 57 commands including PPID spoofing, DPAPI credential extraction from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Local State, timestomping via command 43, and secure file deletion by overwriting with 0, 1, and random bytes before renaming to an alternate data stream (:EFS). ClientHub introduces SNOW 1.0 stream cipher for C2 communications, uses Chromium-style headers (Sec-CH-UA, Sec-Fetch-Mode) to blend with browser traffic, and supports Dropbox as a fallback C2 channel. A browser stealer tool targets Chrome, Edge, and Brave for passwords, cookies, bookmarks, and history.
- The COPPERHEDGE cluster, active in parallel since SyncHole wound down, has been linked to both Gunra ransomware deployment and independent data exfiltration to a dedicated dark web leak site, suggesting a financially motivated sub-cluster operating alongside the espionage-focused FlashHole activity. File hashes for TouchShift (six mscoree.dll variants) and the ClientHub loader (liblzma.dll) are in the report, along with the full IOC table covering file paths under C:\Windows\System32\RasConv\, C:\Windows\System32\DrvConh\, C:\ProgramData\Dell\, and C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\msadc\msadc[.]inc.
Hunt priority: search for mscoree.dll under C:\Windows\System32\RasConv\ and C:\ProgramData\ subdirectories, flag any service whose binary path contains ImeBroker.exe or whose name matches a legitimate netsvcs entry plus two random alpha characters, and look for INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe spawning fsquirt.exe. For C2 detection, monitor outbound GitHub API calls (GET /issues, POST /issues, PATCH /issues) from non-development hosts, and flag Chromium-header HTTP requests to South Korean 🇰🇷 domains from non-browser processes. IOCs and full malware chain details are in the Kaspersky report.

item.title: Recent AI-Assisted Cyber Attacks in Japan: Investigating Attack Infrastructure and Techniques
item.description:
Japan 🇯🇵 faces AI-assisted attacks where threat actors reverse-engineered Android APKs to extract API secrets and exploit SSRF flaws, hitting organizations across multiple countries.
Key findings:
- Attackers used AI to automate vulnerability scanning and API exploitation, a workflow JPCERT/CC confirmed across multiple compromised organizations in Japan 🇯🇵. The attack chain began with reverse engineering Android APK files using open-source tools: Blutter (for AOT-compiled Flutter/Dart binaries) and jadx (for general Android analysis). On the attack servers, investigators found APK files, extraction directories named apk_extract/, and output files such as strings_libapp.txt, indicating the actors were pulling strings from native libapp[.]so libraries to uncover embedded API keys, RSA private keys, and request-signing logic.
- Once API authentication mechanisms were extracted from the compiled binaries, attackers replicated the signing process in standalone Python clients to query production APIs without using the legitimate application. A Python script found on one server functioned as an HTTPS server returning HTTP 302 redirects, consistent with SSRF testing against APIs that follow external URL redirects without destination validation.
- A third server, described as not directly linked to these attacks, contained files associated with targeting MySQL databases, Jenkins servers, and email gateways, alongside EDR evasion tooling and web shells assessed to have been deployed inside victim networks. This suggests the infrastructure spans both initial API exploitation and deeper post-access activity aimed at internal network pivot.
- The three confirmed attack server IPs listed in the report's IoC appendix are: 210.149.87[.]120, 118.26.36[.]16, and 69.10.51[.]162. Targets included web services intended for users outside Japan 🇯🇵, confirming this is not a geographically limited campaign.
Practitioners investigating impacted organizations should hunt for outbound API traffic patterns that bypass normal application flows, particularly requests with valid authentication signatures arriving from IPs not associated with legitimate user clients. Check web server and API gateway logs for anomalous redirect chains and SSRF probe patterns (external URL parameters resolving to internal resources). Review endpoint artifacts for web shells and EDR evasion tooling on internet-facing systems running Jenkins or mail gateway software. If you have infrastructure intelligence related to these servers or connected activity targeting Japanese 🇯🇵 organizations, JPCERT/CC is actively requesting researcher collaboration at info[@]jpcert.or[.]jp. Block the three IoCs above at the network perimeter now.

item.title: Wordfence Argus Discovers High Severity Unauthenticated PHP Object Injection in Duplicator
item.description:
CVE-2026-82814 (CVSS 8.8): Unauthenticated PHP Object Injection in Duplicator and Duplicator Pro allows OS command execution or site takeover via a second-order deserialization flaw triggered during migration. Affects 1M+ active installs.
Technical breakdown:
- CVE-2026-82814 affects Duplicator Free through 1.5.17 and Duplicator Pro through 4.6.10. The root cause is DUPX_UpdateEngine::unserializeTest() calling PHP's native unserialize() without restricting which classes may be instantiated, allowing attacker-supplied class names to trigger __wakeup() and __destruct() methods automatically. The payload can also be base64-encoded, since the migration engine decodes and deserializes base64 content from database columns.
- This is a second-order vulnerability with a multi-step chain. An unauthenticated attacker posts a base64-encoded serialized PHP object as a WordPress comment via the public wp-comments-post.php endpoint, no account or nonce required. The comment is stored in the database even if pending. Nothing fires on submission or package creation. The payload activates only when an administrator later runs a standard migration or import using a package that contains that comment, triggering the Update Data search-and-replace operation.
- The two editions reach different impact. In Duplicator Free, the installed Requests 1.7 library provides a POP chain combining DbUserMode's __wakeup() with Requests_Utility_FilteredIterator, letting the attacker specify any PHP callback and argument, confirmed to achieve OS command execution as the web-server user. In Duplicator Pro, the IndexList destructor's unlink() call enables arbitrary file deletion. Deleting wp-config.php exposes the WordPress setup wizard, and an attacker who reaches it first and supplies a controlled database can create a new administrator and execute PHP code via plugin installation.
- Stored packages do not self-trigger, but they permanently retain the installer from the version that created them. Post-patch testing confirmed that Duplicator Pro 5.0.5's Import workflow ran an older Pro 4.6.10 package installer and hit the vulnerable deserialization path. The fix in version 5.0.0 replaces the unsafe call with SnapUtil::safeUnserialize(), passing ['allowed_classes' => false] to PHP's unserialize() so no attacker-named classes are instantiated. Comment moderation is not a mitigation: unapproved comments are still copied into packages.
- Patch released September 8, 2026. Actively exploited in the wild: not stated in the report. The fix is confirmed in Duplicator Free 5.0.0 and Duplicator Pro 5.0.0 and later.
Practitioner takeaway: Update both Duplicator Free and Duplicator Pro to 5.0.0 or newer immediately. Updating the plugin does not retroactively fix older stored packages. Before using any package created under an affected version for a migration or import, build a fresh package with the updated plugin. Remove any publicly accessible standalone installer files (installer.php) left on disk from previous migrations. To hunt for pre-planted payloads, inspect the wp_comments table in your WordPress database for comment_content containing base64-encoded strings that decode to values beginning with serialized PHP object notation (O: or C:), particularly in comments with comment_approved set to 0 (pending). Those entries should be treated as suspect and removed before any migration is run.

item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-82814 (CVSS 8.8): Unauthenticated PHP Object Injection in Duplicator and Duplicator Pro allows OS command execution or site takeover via a second-order deserialization flaw triggered during migration. Affects 1M+ active installs.

Technical breakdown:

- CVE-2026-82814 affects Duplicator Free through 1.5.17 and Duplicator Pro through 4.6.10. The root cause is DUPX_UpdateEngine::unserializeTest() calling PHP's native unserialize() without restricting which classes may be instantiated, allowing attacker-supplied class names to trigger __wakeup() and __destruct() methods automatically. The payload can also be base64-encoded, since the migration engine decodes and deserializes base64 content from database columns.

- This is a second-order vulnerability with a multi-step chain. An unauthenticated attacker posts a base64-encoded serialized PHP object as a WordPress comment via the public wp-comments-post.php endpoint, no account or nonce required. The comment is stored in the database even if pending. Nothing fires on submission or package creation. The payload activates only when an administrator later runs a standard migration or import using a package that contains that comment, triggering the Update Data search-and-replace operation.

- The two editions reach different impact. In Duplicator Free, the installed Requests 1.7 library provides a POP chain combining DbUserMode's __wakeup() with Requests_Utility_FilteredIterator, letting the attacker specify any PHP callback and argument, confirmed to achieve OS command execution as the web-server user. In Duplicator Pro, the IndexList destructor's unlink() call enables arbitrary file deletion. Deleting wp-config.php exposes the WordPress setup wizard, and an attacker who reaches it first and supplies a controlled database can create a new administrator and execute PHP code via plugin installation.

- Stored packages do not self-trigger, but they permanently retain the installer from the version that created them. Post-patch testing confirmed that Duplicator Pro 5.0.5's Import workflow ran an older Pro 4.6.10 package installer and hit the vulnerable deserialization path. The fix in version 5.0.0 replaces the unsafe call with SnapUtil::safeUnserialize(), passing ['allowed_classes' => false] to PHP's unserialize() so no attacker-named classes are instantiated. Comment moderation is not a mitigation: unapproved comments are still copied into packages.

- Patch released September 8, 2026. Actively exploited in the wild: not stated in the report. The fix is confirmed in Duplicator Free 5.0.0 and Duplicator Pro 5.0.0 and later.

Practitioner takeaway: Update both Duplicator Free and Duplicator Pro to 5.0.0 or newer immediately. Updating the plugin does not retroactively fix older stored packages. Before using any package created under an affected version for a migration or import, build a fresh package with the updated plugin. Remove any publicly accessible standalone installer files (installer.php) left on disk from previous migrations. To hunt for pre-planted payloads, inspect the wp_comments table in your WordPress database for comment_content containing base64-encoded strings that decode to values beginning with serialized PHP object notation (O: or C:), particularly in comments with comment_approved set to 0 (pending). Those entries should be treated as suspect and removed before any migration is run.

item.title: From Phishing to LLMjacking: Threat Actors Targeting Cloud Billing Accounts for LLM Usage
item.description:
LLMjacking hits GCP: threat actors phish cloud admins, hijack billing accounts, and rack up hundreds of thousands in unauthorized Gemini API charges while keeping all AI workloads invisible to victim logs.
Key findings:
- Initial access came through Google Search ads bought against terms like "google cloud" and "gcp". Clicking the ad routed victims through a Google Sites redirect to a credential-harvesting page that captured both passwords and live MFA codes, then silently replayed them to GCP from 212.73.134[.]136. The attacker reauthenticated minutes later from a second IP geolocated inside the victim org's home country, a deliberate blend-in move to suppress location-based alerts.
- Once inside, the attacker enabled the Gemini API in existing low-usage projects, created service accounts with API keys, and assigned those accounts to roles/ml.admin and roles/mcp.toolUser. The organization-level IAM policy iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains was then deleted, lifting the domain restriction and letting external Gmail accounts be granted roles/billing.admin on the victim's billing account.
- The core technique was cross-tenant project linking: attacker-controlled GCP projects were attached directly to the victim's billing account. All Gemini API calls, prompts, and outputs executed in the foreign tenant. The victim's audit logs showed no prompt content, no model output, just a billing spike. Existing internal billing admins were simultaneously demoted to roles/billing.viewer, blocking them from detaching rogue projects via console.
- Within 24 to 48 hours of initial access, victim organizations saw unauthorized Gemini API charges reaching tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The attacker's phishing infrastructure spans a typosquatting network with wildcard subdomains: *.gprokl[.]com, *.gxoosl[.]com, *.gsoolg[.]com, *.gzoozl[.]com (note: no leading dot in source), *.groonl[.]com, *.gsool[.]space, *.gbrokl[.]space, *.gbrokl[.]xyz, *.gsoosl[.]xyz, *.gsool[.]xyz, *.gpoosl[.]com, *.groolg[.]com, *.gcslom[.]com, *.gcoalg[.]com, plus *.gboogl[.]com and *.groosl[.]com.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt GCP Admin Activity and Cloud Billing audit logs for deletion of iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains, grants of roles/billing.admin to external or Gmail accounts, unexpected linking of foreign GCP projects to billing, and service account creation paired with Gemini API enablement in dormant projects. In Google Workspace User Log Events, look for suspicious login flags and anomalous back-to-back reauthentication within minutes, which is the phishing kit replaying harvested credentials. Block the phishing IP 212.73.134[.]136 and the full domain list at your DNS and perimeter layer. The full IOC table is in the Wiz CIRT report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 authenticated command injection in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler, root command execution (7.2)
item.description:
Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 carries an authenticated OS command injection in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler, yielding immediate root execution from a single POST request. CVSS 3.1 score is 7.2 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). No CVE has been assigned.
- The vulnerable handler is registered in bin/webs, an embedded GoAhead-style HTTP server running as uid=0(root) on TCP port 80, via websFormDefine("formWlanMP", ...) at binary offset 0x477a1c. The handler at 0x462a24 reads thirty radio calibration and EEPROM fields through websGetVar, then passes them raw into a single sprintf at 0x462fd0 using a format string of thirty unquoted %s conversions, and hands the result directly to system() at 0x46308c. There is zero validation between source and sink: no character filter, no length check beyond buffer capacity, no argument quoting, no switch to execve. system() forks /bin/sh with -c, so the entire shell grammar is available. A field value of ateFunc=$(id>/tmp/marker) executes the command substitution before shell program lookup, so even though rftest_old.sh is absent from the shipped image and the shell exits 127, the injected command has already run. That exit-127 fingerprint is itself a detection artifact.
- Authentication is required but weak. The route sits behind HTTP Basic authentication tied to a single /etc/boa/boa.passwd realm entry covering all /goform/ paths. There is no lower-privileged role: one realm, one password file, one account. The shipped firmware contains a pre-populated password file (CWE-798) using MD5-crypt, and the model's publicly documented factory credential is admin:1234. There is no rate limiting and no lockout on the Basic challenge, so the single-account realm is permanently exposed to dictionary pressure. The web server declares User root in etc/boa/boa.conf and performs no setuid, chroot, or capability drop. Root before the attack, root after, no escalation required.
- The scope of the problem extends well beyond this one handler. The report counted 91 /goform/form* handlers in the registration table, of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. A companion advisory covers a second independent command injection in the setWAN handler (POST /goform/setWAN, sprintf at 0x441ee8, system() at 0x441f1c), which uses a single-character semicolon filter that a pipe-and-hash payload defeats. The same setWAN implementation was matched instruction-for-instruction against a second Edimax firmware image, suggesting the defect lives in a shared software component.
- Detection is structurally poor. A POST to /goform/formWlanMP with thirty ATE fields is what the vendor's own management page sends, so the request shape is not anomalous. Anomalies to look for are: a non-factory user submitting a factory form, and shell metacharacters ($( backtick semicolon pipe newline) in any of the thirty numeric fields. The most reliable on-device indicator is a shell diagnostic reporting /bin/rftest_old.sh does not exist, the specific fingerprint of this payload reaching this sink. Post-exploitation indicators include unexpected outbound connections originating from the router and DNS resolver changes pushed via DHCP. Marker files written to /tmp are volatile and do not survive a reboot, so a reboot is an anti-forensic step. The vendor's own published materials indicate the BR-series legacy hardware is discontinued and will not receive firmware updates.
Practitioner action: if you are assessing this device, the binary SHA256 for the confirmed vulnerable image is ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1. Until replacement hardware is available, disable remote management, isolate the management interface to a dedicated VLAN, keep guest wireless clients off the management segment, and rotate away from the factory credential immediately. The full technical analysis and a reproducible proof-of-concept tool (Python 3, standard library only, loopback-restricted by default) are published unconditionally at the 0day Rubbish Research Team's site; the companion setWAN advisory and the broader disclosure archive are linked there.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 authenticated command injection in the setWAN WAN-configuration handler, root command execution (7.2)
item.description:
Authenticated command injection in Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 delivers root command execution via a single POST to the WAN configuration handler, with no CVE assigned and no patch coming from a vendor that has publicly discontinued the product.
Technical breakdown:
- The flaw is CWE-78 in the setWAN handler (POST /goform/setWAN) inside bin/webs, a GoAhead-style embedded HTTP server running as uid=0(root) with no privilege drop. The binary is ELF 32-bit big-endian MIPS-I, 762904 bytes, SHA256 ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1. When wanMode is set to 2 (PPP), the pppUserName field from the request is copied into a stack buffer with strcpy, scanned by a single-byte loop that checks only for a semicolon (0x3b), then dropped unquoted into sprintf using the format string "echo %s > /tmp/UserName" and passed directly to system(). Pipe, ampersand, backtick, dollar sign with parentheses, and embedded newline are never inspected. The verified payload is a username of |id > /tmp/marker # which causes the shell to run id and suppress the intended redirect via the trailing comment character. The same injectable pattern exists on the PPTP (pptpUserName, wanMode 3) and L2TP (L2TPUserName, wanMode 6) branches of the same handler: a patch to the PPP path alone leaves two others open. A companion advisory covers a second independent injection in the formWlanMP manufacturing-test handler at POST /goform/formWlanMP, which carries no sanitiser at all across thirty fields.
- The sanitiser audit exposes how far the defense fell short. A hash-escaping loop does exist in this handler, at addresses 0x441f4c to 0x441fb0, but it runs after the system() call at 0x441f1c and operates on the configuration buffer handed to apmib_set, not the buffer handed to the shell. The developer escaped the stored value and left the executed value untouched. CVSS 3.1 score is 7.2 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). Authentication required is High-privilege, one realm, one account, one password file, no lower-privileged role. The report also surfaces a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, whose setWAN implementation is described as instruction-for-instruction identical, suggesting a shared source component across the vendor's router line, though that model was not tested and carries no score in this disclosure.
- The impact at root on this device is broad: all stored secrets are readable, including PPP/PPTP/L2TP ISP and VPN credentials, the administrator password file, wireless PSKs, per-station key material, and any certificate or key on the filesystem. The attacker controls the routing and firewall plane: NAT rules, DNS handed to LAN clients, DHCP, port forwards, wireless SSIDs, and the WAN uplink. Root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, requiring a full reflash for recovery. The shipped firewall script drops WAN-originated SYN, so the default network position for exploitation is a host on the wired LAN or an associated wireless client, including guests; remote management or a port forward moves it to the open internet.
- Detection is structurally difficult because the malicious POST is indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission. The report identifies two usable anomalies. First, a successful injection suppresses creation of /tmp/UserName: a WAN configuration POST that does not create that file when it should is the reliable on-device indicator. Second, the semicolon truncation means an injected payload stores a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, producing a self-inflicted connectivity failure that doubles as a fingerprint. Fields worth logging on any surviving build are those containing a pipe, dollar sign, backtick, hash, or newline in the PPP, PPTP, or L2TP username parameters. /tmp is a tmpfs that does not survive a reboot, so rebooting is an available anti-forensic step.
Practitioner takeaway: No CVE has been assigned and the vendor's own public end-of-service notice states it will not develop new firmware for legacy BR-series hardware, so no patch exists and none is expected. Incident responders and network defenders should treat any BR-6478AC running firmware of this vintage as end-of-life hardware and plan replacement. Until then: change the factory credential (the firmware ships admin:1234 as a published default, documented as CWE-798 in the report), disable remote management and any port forward exposing the management interface, and isolate guest wireless clients from the management subnet, since a guest client holding the management credential is the most direct path to this handler. IOCs, the reproducible Python 3 proof-of-concept, and the full binary analysis are in the report at the 0day-rubbish[.]com URL above.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] TRENDnet TV-IP302PI firmware 1.02.38 authenticated NTP server-address OS command injection to root command execution via a shell-form system() call (7.2 High, PR:H)
item.description:
Unpatched OS command injection in TRENDnet TV-IP302PI firmware 1.02.38 gives an authenticated admin root shell via the NTP server field. CVSS 3.1 score 7.2 High, no CVE assigned yet.
Key details:
- The flaw (CWE-78) lives in the c64_Ntp_Server configuration parameter. The set callback at offset 0x2b668c applies a 48-byte length cap and nothing else: no character filtering, no address parsing. That stored value is later formatted unquoted into the command template "/hunt/msntp -ts %d -r %s &" and handed to system() via the GOT entry at 0xc274, which runs it through /bin/sh -c. A semicolon, backtick pair, or $(...) substitution in what should be a time-server address terminates the msntp invocation and starts an arbitrary command. The daemon runs uid=0(root) with no privilege drop anywhere in its boa configuration, so there is no privilege-escalation step: injection equals root.
- Two entry points write the same slot: HTTP POST to apply.cgi or SetTime.cgi (48-byte cap) and the ONVIF tds:SetNTP handler at offsets 0x286218-0x286264 (64-byte cap). A fix applied only to the HTTP path leaves the ONVIF path open, and the ONVIF cap is the more comfortable carrier for longer payloads. Both paths require valid administrator credentials through a fail-closed HTTP Digest gate, confirmed in the binary's own control flow: this is not CWE-306.
- Exploitation was verified in the vendor's own extracted root filesystem under qemu-arm-static emulation with a chroot, not against physical hardware. Three injection forms (semicolon, command substitution, backtick) each produced a root-owned marker file containing "uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)"; a benign control address 1.1.1.1 produced none. Because the payload is stored in a persisted configuration parameter, it re-executes every time the synchronisation path runs and survives a reboot. No daemon execution was observed directly.
- The daemon binary /hunt/hunt_server carries platform strings including PPPoE_TV-IP302PI and HuntDataDirect, identifying it as built on a Hunt Electronic OEM platform. Other camera models on the same platform may carry identical construction around c64_Ntp_Server. A companion CWE-798 factory credential weakness is disclosed separately; if compounded with a camera still holding its factory password, the conditional CVSS reading reaches 9.8 Critical, but that figure describes two defects together and should not be quoted as the score for this finding.
- Detection is hard because the write is operationally identical to a legitimate NTP configuration change: no failed login, no unusual response code, no privilege change. TRENDnet was notified but delivery could not be confirmed; no CVE has been assigned and no fixed firmware is known to exist. item.content:encoded:
Unpatched OS command injection in TRENDnet TV-IP302PI firmware 1.02.38 gives an authenticated admin root shell via the NTP server field. CVSS 3.1 score 7.2 High, no CVE assigned yet.

Key details:

- The flaw (CWE-78) lives in the c64_Ntp_Server configuration parameter. The set callback at offset 0x2b668c applies a 48-byte length cap and nothing else: no character filtering, no address parsing. That stored value is later formatted unquoted into the command template "/hunt/msntp -ts %d -r %s &" and handed to system() via the GOT entry at 0xc274, which runs it through /bin/sh -c. A semicolon, backtick pair, or $(...) substitution in what should be a time-server address terminates the msntp invocation and starts an arbitrary command. The daemon runs uid=0(root) with no privilege drop anywhere in its boa configuration, so there is no privilege-escalation step: injection equals root.

- Two entry points write the same slot: HTTP POST to apply.cgi or SetTime.cgi (48-byte cap) and the ONVIF tds:SetNTP handler at offsets 0x286218-0x286264 (64-byte cap). A fix applied only to the HTTP path leaves the ONVIF path open, and the ONVIF cap is the more comfortable carrier for longer payloads. Both paths require valid administrator credentials through a fail-closed HTTP Digest gate, confirmed in the binary's own control flow: this is not CWE-306.

- Exploitation was verified in the vendor's own extracted root filesystem under qemu-arm-static emulation with a chroot, not against physical hardware. Three injection forms (semicolon, command substitution, backtick) each produced a root-owned marker file containing "uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)"; a benign control address 1.1.1.1 produced none. Because the payload is stored in a persisted configuration parameter, it re-executes every time the synchronisation path runs and survives a reboot. No daemon execution was observed directly.

- The daemon binary /hunt/hunt_server carries platform strings including PPPoE_TV-IP302PI and HuntDataDirect, identifying it as built on a Hunt Electronic OEM platform. Other camera models on the same platform may carry identical construction around c64_Ntp_Server. A companion CWE-798 factory credential weakness is disclosed separately; if compounded with a camera still holding its factory password, the conditional CVSS reading reaches 9.8 Critical, but that figure describes two defects together and should not be quoted as the score for this finding.

- Detection is hard because the write is operationally identical to a legitimate NTP configuration change: no failed login, no unusual response code, no privilege change. The usable signals are the value itself (audit the stored NTP address on every unit; any value containing shell metacharacters or simply not parsing as a hostname or address is the indicator), unexpected process children of the web daemon (anything other than msntp in that ancestry is anomalous), and outbound connections from the camera to hosts that are not time servers (the trailing ampersand backgrounds the injected command and pushes an attacker toward an outbound callback, which egress filtering will surface).

For responders: restrict camera egress to known time servers, audit the stored NTP field via the camera's own configuration API or management interface, and baseline the web daemon's process tree. If compromise is suspected, re-image and rotate every credential the unit holds: root-level access means both the filesystem and boot image were writable. item.title: [0day-rubbish] Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5-SNAPSHOT anonymous deserialization in the database restore path to JSP command execution as uid=1000 (9.8)
item.description:
Parasoft Continuous Testing Platform 10.7.5-SNAPSHOT carries a publicly disclosed, unpatched 9.8 Critical unauthenticated RCE chain: two HTTP requests, no credentials, no prior setup, arbitrary OS command execution as the product service account.
No CVE has been assigned. No patch exists. The vendor has no public vulnerability disclosure policy and no security.txt. This is a full unconditional public disclosure with working proof of concept.
- Three first-party defects compose into one chain. EMLicenseFilter reads the raw un-normalized request URI and exempts paths matching unanchored suffixes like "welcome" and "about". A servlet container strips semicolon-delimited path parameters before routing, so POST /em/database/restore;welcome bypasses the filter entirely while still landing on the restore handler. That is CWE-436, an interpretation conflict between filter and router. Separately, EMRememberMeServices fails open: when no external security provider is configured (the factory default), any request carrying no Authorization header receives a manufactured ROLE_ADMIN Spring Security principal with authenticated=true, satisfying the authenticated() matcher on /database. That is CWE-287. Combined, an anonymous request to the restore endpoint is both license-gate-bypassed and treated as an authenticated administrator.
- The restore handler in AbstractDatabaseBackup passes an attacker-supplied database.ser zip member directly into an unfiltered ObjectInputStream. The product ships 81 files containing readObject and zero occurrences of ObjectInputFilter, jdk.serialFilter, or serialFilter. The working gadget chain uses commons-collections4 4.5.0 TiedMapEntry to LazyMap forcing a virtual Map.put dispatch into aspectjweaver 1.9.25.1 SimpleCache$StoreableCachingMap, whose writeToPath method concatenates an attacker-controlled folder field with an attacker-controlled key and writes attacker-controlled bytes, with no path validation, no extension constraint, and no content check beyond a four-byte IDEM sentinel. The folder, key, and content all live inside the serialized stream. Classic TemplatesImpl and JdbcRowSetImpl chains are dead on this JDK due to module boundaries; this chain lives entirely in the unnamed module.
- Hop 1 writes a JSP to webapps/em/images/, which is inside the Jasper-mapped web application root, writable by uid 1000, and exempt from the license filter via the contains("/images/") clause, so hop 2 needs no bypass of its own. An anonymous GET to /em/images/<leaf>.jsp executes the shell. The report also measured a second independent execution sink: writing a FreeMarker template to WEB-INF/classes/com/parasoft/rest/api/core/docs/templates/ and invoking freemarker.template.utility.Execute via the new() built-in, returning command output verbatim. A third forensic finding: after the JSP page was deleted and Jasper artefacts were removed, the same URL returned 200 with the compiled servlet still loaded in the JVM. File deletion does not unload the servlet. Only a context reload or container restart does.
- The success signature of hop 1 is a 500 response carrying a routine configuration-error message, not an error indicating compromise. In the product log, look for a stack frame naming AbstractDatabaseBackup.restore(AbstractDatabaseBackup[.]java:114) with "class java.util.HashSet cannot be cast to class...TableMetadata" and a ClassCastException: that proves readObject() returned an object, distinguishing a fired gadget from a malformed payload (ClassNotFoundException) or no attempt at all. Additionally, the product's license refusal path has a dead status write: HTTP status 200 is returned with a JSON body carrying status 403, making license gate hits invisible to any status-based monitoring rule. CVSS 3.1 base score is 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). With an external provider configured and any valid low-privilege account, the score is 8.8.
Hunt now: scan the webapps/em/images/ directory for any non-product JSP files and the Jasper work directory for compiled classes whose stems do not correspond to shipped pages. Search container logs for the ClassCastException stack trace naming AbstractDatabaseBackup at line 114 with a JDK collection class as the cast source. Flag any request URI containing a semicolon reaching /em/database/ or /em/tdm/api/v paths in your proxy or WAF logs. Until a patch exists, block semicolons in request targets at the gateway, restrict /em/database and /em/tdm/api to named management addresses behind an authenticating proxy, and if remediating a confirmed drop, restart the container before hunting lateral movement through the platform's stored credentials and HSQLDB database files. The full proof of concept and technical analysis are in the report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Exasol Database 7.1.30 docker-db form: shipped default SYS credential to PYTHON3 UDF os.popen command execution as uid=500(exadefusr), output returned in-band (8.8)
item.description:
Exasol Database 7.1.30 docker-db ships a documented default SYS credential (sys / exasol) that chains directly into an unrestricted PYTHON3 UDF engine, giving any adjacent attacker OS command execution with output returned in-band. CVSS 3.1: 8.8 High; no CVE assigned yet.
- The two-leg chain requires no provisioning decision. Leg one: the credential sys / exasol is printed in the vendor's own README and hardcoded in image-internal CI scripts at /usr/opt/EXASuite-7/EXAClusterOS-7.1.30/docker/test/basic_test.sh and basic_sc_test.sh. Nothing in the container's start path rotates it: the controller carries no -defaultSysPasswordHash argument, EXAConf carries no DefaultSysPasswdHash key, and there is no forced first-login gate. Crucially, db_jobs.py:104 generates a random via secrets.token_hex(20) but that becomes an additional accepted password, not a replacement, so the constant remains valid. Leg two: once authenticated as SYS, CREATE OR REPLACE PYTHON3 SCALAR SCRIPT with an os.popen call is valid SQL, the os module is importable with no allow-list or capability gate, and the SELECT result set carries the command's stdout back to the caller in-band, removing any need for an egress channel.
- Execution identity and namespace: the UDF runs as uid=500(exadefusr) gid=500(exausers) groups=500(exausers),0(root). Root appears as a supplementary group only; no escalation to uid=0 was attempted or claimed. The UDF runs in a separate mount namespace (a file written inside did not appear in the container's filesystem view), but uname returned the host kernel 5.10.134-19.2.al8.x86_64, confirming kernel sharing. The container must run --privileged per the vendor's README for UDF support, so this is the documented deployment posture.
- Network reachability and scoring. The headline 8.8 (AV:A) reflects that the vendor's stand-alone quickstart publishes port 8563 loopback-only (127.0.0.1:9563:8563). Under --network=host or any operator publication without a loopback restriction, the conditional score rises to 9.8 Critical (AV:N). Under default bridge networking with no explicit port publication, the port is reachable from the host and every container on the same bridge, which is the logically adjacent topology the headline score captures. No CVE has been assigned; no fix is planned for this deployment form as the vendor has declared it unsupported.
- Detection is structurally weak. Every step is legitimate product behaviour: a TLS handshake on 8563, a SYS login, script creation, and a SELECT. The only durable artifact the attack leaves is the schema and PYTHON3 script object created by the attacker, which persists across sessions and is enumerable with ordinary SQL. The attack payload uses CREATE OR REPLACE, so repeated execution rewrites one object rather than accumulating new ones, defeating volume-based alerting. Authentication failures ([28000] authentication failed) on port 8563 against the sys user are the second-best signal; no rate limit or lockout was observed on SQL authentication.
DFIR action: query the database's script-object catalog for any PYTHON3, LUA, JAVA, or R scalar scripts owned by SYS or created from unexpected source addresses, and treat presence of any such object in a deployment that was never known to use UDFs as a high-priority finding. Audit records for script-object creation (creating user plus source address) are the highest-value signal and are absent from the default deployment. For any instance still answering sys / exasol on port 8563, treat it as compromised until audited: the credential is public, its use leaves no distinguishing trace from a legitimate admin session, and the attacker can create additional accounts through the SQL channel that survive credential rotation. Rotate the SYS password immediately; that single change moves the finding from 8.8 to not applicable where no other account holds script-creation rights.

item.title: BRONZE SANDCASTLE deploys modified Meterpreter shells
item.description:
Chinese-nexus BRONZE SANDCASTLE targets Asia and Africa with a modified Meterpreter-based implant delivered via Sandboxie DLL sideloading, active August 2025 through August 2026.
Key findings:
- BRONZE SANDCASTLE's defining signature is DLL sideloading using legitimate executables (SandboxieWUAU.exe, javaw.exe, Krita.exe, bginfo64.exe, and others) paired with malicious DLLs that read and execute payloads from encrypted config.ini files on disk. The clean loader, malicious DLL, and encrypted payload are often bundled together in a ZIP archive (aez[.]zip was one observed example), keeping disk artifacts minimal and static detection largely ineffective.
- The decrypted payload is a custom backdoor with structural similarities to stageless Metasploit shellcode, including position-independent execution and in-memory PE loading, but it is not standard MSF output. API resolution uses non-standard hashing rather than Metasploit's well-known ROR13 algorithm, and the codebase is substantially larger. It also incorporates COFFLoader elements, pointing to a custom Beacon Object File for post-exploitation capability. Two versions were identified: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7.
- C2 infrastructure blends into legitimate traffic. Version 1.1.5 contacted dc.cathaypacifice[.]com and net.dpworldto[.]com. Version 1.1.7 communicated with github[.]com repositories (hxxps://api.github[.]com/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW) to pull encrypted config files disguised as .js.map and README[.]md files. The payload also reached out to file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io for possible C2 tasking.
- On-host post-compromise activity includes Windows "net" commands for network and user enumeration, followed by ntds.dit theft: threat actors created Volume Shadow Copies via vssadmin.exe before copying the Active Directory database, giving them the full credential store of the targeted domain.
- Victims span the Philippines 🇵🇭, Taiwan 🇹🇼, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely the Republic of Korea. Operator activity clusters in UTC+8 working hours, consistent with China-based attribution. CTU created the BRONZE SANDCASTLE designation because the technical profile is distinct from overlapping groups BRONZE PRESIDENT and BRONZE ATLAS despite similar geographic targeting.
Practitioner takeaway: static file detection will miss this threat because the payload lives only in memory after decryption. Hunt for DLL loads followed by immediate in-memory shellcode activity, anomalous PE headers in process memory, and reflective loading patterns. Watch for vssadmin.exe creating shadow copies alongside LSASS or ntds.dit access, and flag outbound connections from unusual parent processes to github[.]com, file[.]io, or ably[.]io. Sophos detections ATK/Swrort-Y, ATK/ScLoad-W through ATK/ScLoad-Z, Troj/Loader-JL, and Troj/Loader-JP cover known samples. The full IOC list is in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

item.title: Fake Kernel Threads Are Hiding Backdoors on Linux Servers and Appliances
item.description:
Fake kernel threads are hiding active backdoors across Linux servers and appliances. Four malware families in 2026 use T1036.004 to blend into process lists, and network appliances make detection painfully hard.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-75650 (CVSS 10.0, Critical, actively exploited as a zero-day) let attackers plant the StyleSmuggler Rust backdoor on Magento and Adobe Commerce stores. Early samples ran as [kworker/u:8:0], a name the kernel would never actually produce: real unbound kworkers follow the format kworker/u8:2, so the missing pool digit and extra colon flag it immediately. Within one day of Sansec's September 5 disclosure, samples had already pivoted to fc-cache and chronyd, showing how fast a name-based detection decays.
- A separate Cyclops Blink variant, attributed to the cluster UAT-11823 overlapping with Sandworm, hit Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center via CVE-2026-20079 (CVSS 10.0, Critical authentication bypass granting root). Talos confirmed the payload is an ELF binary dropped on the FMC appliance OS. FMC gives administrators no root shell and accepts no EDR agent, so process-level checks cannot run there without vendor-supported tooling.
- The masquerade only works at the surface. Real kernel threads are parented to kthreadd (PID 2), show zero in VSZ and RSS, have no executable behind /proc/PID/exe, carry the PF_KTHREAD flag, own no network sockets, and have an empty /proc/PID/cmdline. A process whose comm or args contains a literal bracket character put it there itself: ps adds the brackets when the cmdline is empty. Every malware family in this report runs in user space and fails at least one of these checks.
- Persistence varies by family. StyleSmuggler uses a cron job restarting the implant twice hourly. The OpenCart Go C2 agent (watchdogd, disguised as [kworker/7:2]) used an [@]reboot cron entry plus a five-minute restart job. Tengu installs a systemd service labelled "System Helper Service," SysV init scripts, OpenWrt procd entries, and /etc/rc.local. Talos lists /etc/init.d/ scripts as a Cyclops Blink persistence capability. Killing the process without clearing persistence brings it straight back.
Practitioner takeaway: run the report's shell one-liner as root to get a first pass: ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,vsz,rss,comm,args | grep -E '\[(kworker|ksoftirqd|kswapd|migration|rcu_)'
Real kernel threads show ppid=2, user=root, VSZ=0, RSS=0. Anything else is worth escalating. The report also includes a /proc-walking bash script that reads /proc/PID/exe via readlink and prints SUSPECT lines for any process claiming a kernel-thread name while backed by a file on disk. item.content:encoded:
Fake kernel threads are hiding active backdoors across Linux servers and appliances. Four malware families in 2026 use T1036.004 to blend into process lists, and network appliances make detection painfully hard.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-75650 (CVSS 10.0, Critical, actively exploited as a zero-day) let attackers plant the StyleSmuggler Rust backdoor on Magento and Adobe Commerce stores. Early samples ran as [kworker/u:8:0], a name the kernel would never actually produce: real unbound kworkers follow the format kworker/u8:2, so the missing pool digit and extra colon flag it immediately. Within one day of Sansec's September 5 disclosure, samples had already pivoted to fc-cache and chronyd, showing how fast a name-based detection decays.

- A separate Cyclops Blink variant, attributed to the cluster UAT-11823 overlapping with Sandworm, hit Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center via CVE-2026-20079 (CVSS 10.0, Critical authentication bypass granting root). Talos confirmed the payload is an ELF binary dropped on the FMC appliance OS. FMC gives administrators no root shell and accepts no EDR agent, so process-level checks cannot run there without vendor-supported tooling.

- The masquerade only works at the surface. Real kernel threads are parented to kthreadd (PID 2), show zero in VSZ and RSS, have no executable behind /proc/PID/exe, carry the PF_KTHREAD flag, own no network sockets, and have an empty /proc/PID/cmdline. A process whose comm or args contains a literal bracket character put it there itself: ps adds the brackets when the cmdline is empty. Every malware family in this report runs in user space and fails at least one of these checks.

- Persistence varies by family. StyleSmuggler uses a cron job restarting the implant twice hourly. The OpenCart Go C2 agent (watchdogd, disguised as [kworker/7:2]) used an [@]reboot cron entry plus a five-minute restart job. Tengu installs a systemd service labelled "System Helper Service," SysV init scripts, OpenWrt procd entries, and /etc/rc.local. Talos lists /etc/init.d/ scripts as a Cyclops Blink persistence capability. Killing the process without clearing persistence brings it straight back.

Practitioner takeaway: run the report's shell one-liner as root to get a first pass:
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,vsz,rss,comm,args | grep -E '\[(kworker|ksoftirqd|kswapd|migration|rcu_)'

Real kernel threads show ppid=2, user=root, VSZ=0, RSS=0. Anything else is worth escalating. The report also includes a /proc-walking bash script that reads /proc/PID/exe via readlink and prints SUSPECT lines for any process claiming a kernel-thread name while backed by a file on disk. Before killing a confirmed hit, collect /proc/PID/exe, /proc/PID/environ, /proc/PID/cwd, and network socket output from ss. For Adobe Commerce, patch APSB26-146 and assume customer order data was exposed. For FMC, ask your vendor contact what process visibility is available under CVE-2026-20079 remediation.

item.title: Inside Wazza: A Newly Observed Device Code Phishing Kit Targeting Microsoft 365 Accounts
item.description:
Wazza, a newly observed multi-stage device code phishing kit, has been actively targeting Microsoft 365 accounts since at least July 2026, using compromised email accounts, Google Sites wrappers, Cloudflare Workers, and .EU domains to deliver OAuth token theft at scale.
Key findings:
- The attack chain runs four distinct stages: a business-themed PDF lure (invoice, contract, urgent review) sent from compromised accounts links victims to a Google Sites wrapper or directly to .EU phishing domains, which load the 56 KB Wazza preloader script. That script initializes campaign parameters (tgm, m, tg, thm), performs beacon synchronization against beacon-surge-sync.beacon-surge-sync.workers[.]dev or beaconoflinenew.lastfightlink.workers[.]dev, generates a victim-specific routing token via /api/mint-token, then redirects through subdomains (check, id, gate, later portal, hub, svc) before a Cloudflare Workers-hosted final page completes the device code theft. The kit impersonates Adobe, DocuSign, and Microsoft OneDrive, and its tg parameter carries XOR-decoded, Base62-encoded victim data including email address, company name, and document filename.
- The protection stack is deliberately layered to defeat automated analysis: c.js checks for Selenium, WebDriver, Puppeteer, Playwright, PhantomJS, and headless user-agent strings, then encrypts collected browser fingerprint data with PBKDF2-SHA256 (100,000 iterations) and AES-256-GCM before submitting it as a browser challenge. KPSDK intercepts same-origin POST requests and injects the result into the x-is-human header. A Cloudflare Turnstile challenge precedes backend session initialization, and the /api/wazza-config endpoint gates which subdomain prefixes may proceed through the phishing workflow at all.
- Device code phishing is the payload, not a credential harvester. The final Workers-hosted page calls the Microsoft OAuth device authorization endpoint (login.microsoftonline[.]com/.../oauth2/deviceauth), presents the returned code as a document verification code, and polls /api.php?svc=svcm&action=status every two seconds watching for wzzmued:"yes" or wzzmstate:"used". When the victim authenticates, the backend marks the session complete and the attacker holds a valid OAuth access token, bypassing MFA entirely. The kit already shows three service variants: svcm (default), svco (OneDrive), and svcd (DocuSign), confirming active development.
- Wazza's modular design carries 19 phishing themes and six rotating corporate decoy personas (Veltmann & Cie., Kellner & Brandt, Praevita Klinik, Arenberg Residences, Taktiv, Nordlys Energy) selected by hour via Date[.]now(), meaning the same infrastructure presents a different legitimate-looking organization depending on when it is visited, a direct sandbox-evasion technique. The second wave dropped the decoy homepage logic and hardened subdomain routing, showing operators actively iterating the kit.
- Infrastructure IOCs include hutspotmaken[.]eu as an observed core Wazza domain and a full table of .EU and .COM phishing domains plus long-format workers[.]dev final-stage domains (e.g. wndws-pip3ln-sql3-waf3-purv3-gdprsx-dfn-azfn-appsvc-0ffapx.workers[.]dev) in the report. For detection, hunt proxy and DNS logs for the URL parameters tok, tgm, m, tg, thm, and ch appearing together; flag requests to /api/wazza-config, /api/mint-token, /api/fire-mint, /api/klam-kadity, /api/queltz-narvik, /bb-landing, and /api.php?svc= endpoints; and alert on redirect paths /r?key=, /meline, /onlsbdmn, /onfqdn, /eprfx, and /prfxmsmach. Correlate Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs for device code grant completions that occur within minutes of a user opening a PDF attachment or visiting an unfamiliar document-sharing URL. Disable the device code flow in Entra ID where it is not operationally required, or scope it with Conditional Access to managed devices and trusted locations.

item.title: Dissecting the ax-llm CVEs: Why Edge AI Memory and Execution Boundaries Matter
item.description:
Seven CVEs across the ax-llm edge AI inference runtime expose AXERA-TECH silicon to RCE, DMA memory corruption, and OS command injection on smart cameras, automotive ADAS, and industrial controllers running AX8850 and AX650 chips.
Key findings:
- Cobalt's offensive research team audited ax-llm, the open-source C++ inference engine AXERA-TECH ships with its AX8850 and AX650 silicon. The company has raised $379M and ships into automotive driver-assistance, smart camera, and factory automation supply chains. Seven CVE candidates were submitted to MITRE with formal publication scheduled for October 31, 2026. AXERA-TECH pushed fixes across commits 5ad6f17, 47405d2, 23faad8, and 5dce054, but upstream commits do not update hardware in the field. Coordinated disclosure began July 18, 2026; GitHub issues were filed September 21, 2026.
- The most critical finding is CAN-2026-2038801 (CVSS v3.1 8.4, CWE-78), an OS command injection in src/runner/utils/audio_processor.cpp. The audio preprocessor passed caller-supplied filenames unsanitized into snprintf and then _popen, giving any caller who can influence audio_path immediate shell execution as the inference daemon. Because edge daemons run as root to issue ioctl calls against /dev/ax_npu and manage PCIe accelerators, this collapses to unauthenticated RCE with full device privileges. The commit 5dce054 added shell_quote() escaping. Defenders should check whether deployed BSPs pulled that commit.
- CAN-2026-2038776 (CVSS v3.1 7.1, CWE-787 chained to CWE-190) and CAN-2026-2038777 (CVSS v3.1 7.1) both write past allocated CMM/MMZ physical memory buffers in src/runner/LLM_decode.cpp and LLM_embed.cpp. The DMA attention mask copy in LLM.hpp trusted caller-supplied vector length with no destination bounds check against input_mask.nSize. The position index fill loop in LLM_decode.cpp wrote input_num_token integers past idx_elems without clamping. Both produced garbled Mojibake token output immediately before a kernel driver fault locked the PCIe NPU bus, requiring a physical power cycle to recover. This is the forensic signature: corrupted inference output followed by /dev/ax_npu driver fault and bus lockup.
- CAN-2026-2034987 (CVSS v3.1 7.3, CWE-120/CWE-134) is a stack buffer overflow in src/runner/LLM_init.cpp. The shard path loader used unbounded sprintf into a fixed 1024-byte stack buffer, with the format string drawn from a model's config.json. A crafted model package with an oversized format specifier like %02048d overwrites saved return addresses. On embedded toolchains that strip stack canaries to save flash, this lands execution control directly. The artifact here is a malicious config.json inside a distributed .axmodel package: model supply chain poisoning is an explicit attack path the report documents under T1195.002.
- CAN-2026-2038778 (CVSS v3.1 7.5, CWE-190/CWE-122) sits in src/runner/utils/image_processor.cpp. Signed 32-bit stride multiplication in resize_pillow() and create_patches() wraps on image widths above 536,870,911 pixels. A negative wraparound cast to size_t requests petabyte allocations and throws std::bad_alloc; a positive wraparound allocates a tiny heap buffer that the pixel copy loop immediately overflows. Any network-exposed multimodal endpoint accepting image input is reachable here via T1190. CAN-2026-2038779 (CVSS v3.1 6.2, CWE-415) in src/cmdline.hpp is a Rule-of-Three double-free in the CLI parser: the class frees raw option_base heap pointers in its destructor without defining a copy constructor, so shallow copies corrupt glibc tcache freelists.
DFIR takeaway: The immediate hunt is firmware provenance. Pull the commit hash of the ax-llm BSP integrated into your edge appliances and compare against the four remediation commits (5ad6f17, 47405d2, 23faad8, 5dce054). If deployed firmware predates those commits, treat the device as compromised-capable and prioritize isolation, particularly any unit running multimodal audio or image ingestion. On a device you can inspect, look for /dev/ax_npu driver fault messages and garbled token output in inference logs as the observable indicator of the DMA corruption chain. The report's CWE and ATT&CK mappings (T1190, T1195.002, T1068, T1499.001) are in the Cobalt advisory for detection engineering alignment. Formal CVE records publish October 31, 2026.

item.title: mtt.sh: Mounting Linux Images
item.description:
mtt[.]sh automates forensically sound mounting of complex Linux disk images, handling RAID, LVM, and mixed file systems that routinely defeat commercial tools, with full audit trail generation.
Key details:
- The script handles multi-disk E01, VMDK, and raw images containing Linux software RAID (mdadm), LVM volume groups, and mixed file systems including EXT4 and XFS, including "dirty" images with incomplete journal transactions. It mounts everything read-only with noexec and norecovery/noload mount options, preserving forensic integrity. Every exact command used is written to a MOUNTING text file in the target directory, giving examiners a complete, reproducible audit trail of how the image was accessed.
- The -E flag exports each mounted logical volume as a separate E01 with a companion .txt acquisition log containing the MD5 hash of the logical image. This is the bridge for teams who need to hand off Linux file systems to commercial tools: instead of fighting with RAID and LVM reconstruction, analysts get discrete, hash-verified images of root, boot, and home volumes ready to load directly.
- Duplicate UUID and LVM volume group name collisions are a real-world headache when multiple images were cloned from the same master. The -V flag renames the volume group; the -A flag changes both the LVM name and all significant UUIDs. Both options use xmount to create a writable cache file in front of the original images so changes never touch the source evidence. Be aware: -A must replay dirty journals read-write to clear them before UUID changes can proceed, meaning the mounted file system may reflect post-recovery state rather than the raw dirty state.
- The -W flag mounts the image read-write against a cache file only, useful for controlled experimentation or triage without touching source data. Like -A, it clears journal transactions as a side effect, so what you see reflects post-reboot state. The -U flag handles full teardown in reverse order: LVM deactivation, RAID array stop, loopback disconnect, and ewfmount unmount.
Takeaway: for any Linux investigation involving RAID or LVM, the MOUNTING file mtt[.]sh drops in the target directory is your court-ready record of exactly how the image was accessed, mount options included. The script is available at github[.]com/halpomeranz/dfis. Dependencies are qemu-utils, ewf-tools, and xmount, installable via apt.

item.title: CVE-2026-106173 Deep-Dive: FortiSIEM gRPC Path Traversal File Write RCE
item.description:
CVE-2026-106173: Unauthenticated gRPC path traversal on FortiSIEM enables arbitrary file write and RCE. Fortinet published the advisory on 13 October 2026; Horizon3[.]ai has released a proof of concept on GitHub.
Key details:
- The vulnerable service is phQueryMaster, listening on tcp/27918 across all interfaces. The gRPC server is configured with GRPC_SSL_DONT_REQUEST_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE, meaning any remote client reaches it with no authentication and no client certificate required. The RPC method SendQueryResult accepts streamed bytes and a metadata block that includes query-id and src-ip, both attacker-controlled.
- Bug 1 is a directory traversal: the server builds the output path by string-concatenating query-id directly into /query/result/ with zero input validation. A query-id of ../../../../../tmp/x lands the file anywhere on the filesystem the process can write. Bug 2 is null-byte injection in the header: because the server copies the declared length of the value rather than stopping at a null byte, embedding \0 in the middle of a path causes the OS to discard everything after it, including the server-appended result-..-.dat suffix. This gives the attacker full filename control, not just directory control.
- The exploitation path to RCE chains both bugs: traverse to /opt/charting/redishb.sh, embed a null byte to strip the server suffix, and stream a malicious shell script as the file content. A cron job invokes redishb[.]sh every 60 seconds to perform redis health checks, so code execution follows within a minute. A second file of interest noted in the report is /opt/phoenix/bin/phLicenseTool.
- Horizon3[.]ai explicitly states they found no application log entries that directly record exploitation of this vulnerability. The only host-based signal is filesystem metadata: file write and modification timestamps on overwritten scripts that do not align with the surrounding files in the same directory.
DFIR angle: Fortinet advisory and Horizon3[.]ai PoC are both public, so treat this as actively exploitable now. On any FortiSIEM appliance, pull filesystem metadata for /opt/charting/redishb.sh and /opt/phoenix/bin/phLicenseTool and compare mtime against neighboring files and expected deployment baselines. A timestamp that is anomalously recent or that stands out from the directory's surrounding entries is the primary indicator. Because no log source captures the write event itself, file integrity is your only forensic surface here. Network-side, look for unexpected inbound connections to tcp/27918 from sources that are not legitimate FortiSIEM cluster peers. Apply Fortinet's patch; without it, the service is reachable and writable by any unauthenticated host that can reach port 27918.

Apply Fortinet's patch; without it, the service is reachable and writable by any unauthenticated host that can reach port 27918.

item.title: INC and The Gentlemen Ransomware: Exposed AI Infrastructure
item.description:
Russian-speaking ransomware affiliates built an AI-orchestrated intrusion platform exposed by their own OPSEC failures, revealing 46 staged encryptors, 62 named victims, and the source code of a novel autonomous attack framework called Phantom.
Key findings:
- Seven adversary servers were exposed, anchored at 45.227.254[.]43, which held OpenCode AI session logs (8,257 messages across 133 sessions, over $23,920 spent on OpenRouter API access using models including anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 and moonshotai/kimi-k3), a persistent victim-tracking knowledge base, and the full source of Phantom: a modular 18-skill "Autonomous Red Team Kill Chain Framework" with Python and Go agents that masquerade as Windows Update components and beacon to api.iquickline[.]com. The AI planned reconnaissance, generated commands, triaged exfiltrated data and drafted extortion material. Humans approved each step. When commercial models refused a request, operators reframed it as an "Authorized Red Team Assessment Request" rather than switching to an uncensored model. The knowledge base and session logs form a complete, timestamped evidence trail of the campaign.
- Initial access centered on three CVEs actively exploited at scale per operator records: CVE-2026-35616 (FortiClient EMS auth bypass, 2,236 targets, 108 backdoor admin accounts created, 4,140 managed endpoints reachable), CVE-2024-57727 (SimpleHelp path traversal, 4,922 servers scanned, 427 admin passwords stolen, 242 unique IPs impacted), and CVE-2026-41940 (cPanel/WHM auth bypass, 49+ claimed breaches used as springboards to hosted mail infrastructure). MSP credential theft was a major force multiplier: one reused password unlocked VPN, RMM, backup, and security management simultaneously. The operators also attempted ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472), PrintNightmare, noPac, and a PAN-OS User-ID buffer overflow, with mixed results recorded in their own logs.
- The custom arsenal recovered in source and binary form includes Phantom (18-skill autonomous framework), Ghost C2 (three polymorphic generations over HTTPS via Cloudflare, Telegram, or DNS), RevSocks (reverse SOCKS5 pivot, host 77.110.109[.]248), a Quick Heal/Seqrite BYOVD killer abusing the Zemana driver, a Cloudflare-fronted Mythic agent named QuickLine (C2 zone iquickline[.]com), and rks3/BackupAgent exfiltration tools. Persistence for the phishing delivery component used a scheduled task named RealtekAudioSvc. The partner onboarding guide on 45.227.254[.]45 advertises 35 MCP servers, 55+ tools, and a 9,000+ CVE PoC library, pointing to a tooling-provider model serving multiple ransomware affiliates.
- 46 INC encryptor builds (Windows and Linux) were staged for six named victims and packed for an October 1, 2026 deployment wave. A SimpleHelp screenshot from September 30 shows live encryption running on a victim workstation. The Windows encryptor stops backup and database services, removes shadow copies via IOCTL 0x0053C028 (not vssadmin), appends .INC, and drops INC-README.txt. The extortion playbook prefers data leverage over encryption pressure: operators estimate payment capacity from stolen financials, send proof samples, open without a price demand, then escalate through vishing calls, regulator notifications, customer-facing look-alike sites (trulitesupport[.]com warned Trulite's customers directly), and publication. Payment was planned in Monero. 62 organizations are named in operator records, 36 in the United States 🇺🇸, led by industrial/manufacturing (16.1%) and healthcare (14.5%).
- The FOFA scanning accounts were tied to smilefacesec[@]gmail[.]com, linked to a BreachForums account "sm4l1st123". Most infrastructure runs on AS267784 (Flyservers S.A.). Operator activity patterns indicate Russian-speaking operators active primarily 06:00 to 14:00 UTC.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt your FortiClient EMS console now for accounts matching the sysadmin, fct_svc_*, or ems_monitor_* naming patterns, and audit VPN on_connect scripts for unauthorized modifications. In endpoint telemetry, watch for Zemana driver loads paired with Quick Heal or Seqrite service termination, Restart Manager sessions from non-installer processes, volume handle opens followed by IOCTL 0x0053C028, and mass renames to .INC. For C2 and tunneling, flag outbound connections to system-strategy[.]org, iquickline[.]com, mcgrawney[.]com, cloud-update[.]live, and bossprotect[.]com, and look for RevSocks/Chisel/Ligolo traffic patterns. In AD, alert on replication requests from non-DC hosts and shadow-copy access to ntds.dit. The nine INC encryptor SHA-256 hashes and the full extended IOC list are in the SOCRadar report and platform; the complete whitepaper covers tooling internals and encryptor analysis.
