item.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: What Detection Teams Should Actually Hunt
item.description:
BYOVD is not one technique, it is four. Detection teams writing a single "EDR killer" rule are leaving three kill paths completely unmonitored.
The core problem is a taxonomy failure. "EDR killer" collapses four distinct attack classes into one label, and one driver-load rule catches only one of them. Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver, bring-your-own-installer, admin-to-kernel, and driverless suspension share a goal and almost nothing else. The bring-your-own-installer and driverless paths never load a driver at all, so that single rule fires on nothing while the agent dies.
- Bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver is the loudest path and the first to instrument. Sysmon Event ID 6 logs every driver load with ImageLoaded, Hashes, Signed, Signature, and SignatureStatus. Any SignatureStatus other than Valid warrants investigation. Build two rules: one alerting on invalid signature status, one alerting on a first-seen driver hash or signer. The real strength is the correlation chain: sc.exe service create (Sysmon Event ID 1) plus System Event 7045, then Event ID 6, then a DeviceIoControl IOCTL to the freshly-loaded driver, in a tight time window. That ordered sequence is a fingerprint ordinary administration does not produce. A "KB"-style service name joined to an unsigned or first-seen driver image is a high-confidence pair on its own. POORTRY, carrying valid WHQL signatures later revoked under advisory ADV220005, is the canonical signed-driver kill primitive this hunt is built to catch. The same driver-load-then-kill chain appears across Kasseika, BlackByte, and RansomHub campaigns.
- Admin-to-kernel and kernel-callback removal require a different lens entirely, because the kill can happen below the EDR's user-mode vantage point. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write alongside hlpdrv.sys for kernel-callback manipulation, removing EDR callbacks across more than 300 products. The same rwdrv.sys plus hlpdrv.sys pairing appears in Akira operations. The observable is the silent disappearance of kernel callbacks from the EDR's own integrity reporting. A secondary behavioral fingerprint follows: a user-mode loop enumerating PIDs and sending them via IOCTL to a kernel service, which calls ZwTerminateProcess on a fixed interval, bypassing protected-process light. A security agent that respawns and dies again on a repeating, fixed cadence is being killed from below, not crashing on its own.
- Bring-your-own-installer never loads a vulnerable driver, so no Event ID 6 fires. The hunt is an unexpected agent upgrade, reinstall, or version change outside sanctioned change windows. This requires a clean baseline of approved upgrade windows and package signers. Any deviation is the finding. Driverless suspension splits into two sub-paths: EDR-Freeze races the WerFaultSecure crash handler to suspend the agent process entirely in user mode, and EDRSilencer adds Windows Filtering Platform filters to silently drop agent telemetry egress across roughly 16 products. Hunt process-suspension state changes against the agent process that no maintenance action requested, and watch for new WFP filters matching the agent's known egress destinations.
- When the kill succeeds, you are still not blind. Scope a dedicated rule to Windows Event ID 7031 (service terminated unexpectedly) against security services: it is quiet enough to alert on directly and a forced kernel termination often leaves this trail even when it succeeds. Then treat heartbeat loss and absent telemetry as alertable signals. Cross-domain telemetry survives the kill: firewall logs, identity provider logs, and cloud control plane activity record lateral movement, credential use, and C2 that precede ransomware regardless of whether the endpoint sensor is alive. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore 🇸🇬 documents the EDR-killer-then-ransomware sequence across multiple gangs, with encryption following shortly after the kill. The minutes between kill and encryption are a live intervention window, not a post-incident artifact. AvNeutralizer (also called AuKill), traced to FIN7 and sold on Russian-language forums for $4,000 to $15,000, was adopted by Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit. EDRKillShifter entered the RansomHub affiliate program. This is a market, not a single actor, so the hunts must generalize across tools.
Sequence the rollout by signal quality: ship the Sysmon Event ID 6 untrusted-driver and first-seen rules first, add the service-create-to-driver-load-to-IOCTL correlation second, then add the Event ID 7031 and heartbeat-loss rules once change-window baselines are clean. Shipping absence-of-signal detection before that baseline exists floods the queue and trains analysts to ignore it. IOC lists for POORTRY and the LOLDrivers project are in the public loldrivers[.]io catalog.

POORTRY, carrying valid WHQL signatures later revoked under advisory ADV220005, is the canonical signed-driver kill primitive this hunt is built to catch. The same driver-load-then-kill chain appears across Kasseika, BlackByte, and RansomHub campaigns.

- Admin-to-kernel and kernel-callback removal require a different lens entirely, because the kill can happen below the EDR's user-mode vantage point. SOC Prime documented Qilin loading rwdrv.sys for raw memory read and write alongside hlpdrv.sys for kernel-callback manipulation, removing EDR callbacks across more than 300 products. The same rwdrv.sys plus hlpdrv.sys pairing appears in Akira operations. The observable is the silent disappearance of kernel callbacks from the EDR's own integrity reporting. A secondary behavioral fingerprint follows: a user-mode loop enumerating PIDs and sending them via IOCTL to a kernel service, which calls ZwTerminateProcess on a fixed interval, bypassing protected-process light. A security agent that respawns and dies again on a repeating, fixed cadence is being killed from below, not crashing on its own.

- Bring-your-own-installer never loads a vulnerable driver, so no Event ID 6 fires. The hunt is an unexpected agent upgrade, reinstall, or version change outside sanctioned change windows. This requires a clean baseline of approved upgrade windows and package signers. Any deviation is the finding. Driverless suspension splits into two sub-paths: EDR-Freeze races the WerFaultSecure crash handler to suspend the agent process entirely in user mode, and EDRSilencer adds Windows Filtering Platform filters to silently drop agent telemetry egress across roughly 16 products. Hunt process-suspension state changes against the agent process that no maintenance action requested, and watch for new WFP filters matching the agent's known egress destinations.

- When the kill succeeds, you are still not blind. Scope a dedicated rule to Windows Event ID 7031 (service terminated unexpectedly) against security services: it is quiet enough to alert on directly and a forced kernel termination often leaves this trail even when it succeeds. Then treat heartbeat loss and absent telemetry as alertable signals. Cross-domain telemetry survives the kill: firewall logs, identity provider logs, and cloud control plane activity record lateral movement, credential use, and C2 that precede ransomware regardless of whether the endpoint sensor is alive. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore 🇸🇬 documents the EDR-killer-then-ransomware sequence across multiple gangs, with encryption following shortly after the kill. The minutes between kill and encryption are a live intervention window, not a post-incident artifact. AvNeutralizer (also called AuKill), traced to FIN7 and sold on Russian-language forums for $4,000 to $15,000, was adopted by Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit. EDRKillShifter entered the RansomHub affiliate program. This is a market, not a single actor, so the hunts must generalize across tools.

Sequence the rollout by signal quality: ship the Sysmon Event ID 6 untrusted-driver and first-seen rules first, add the service-create-to-driver-load-to-IOCTL correlation second, then add the Event ID 7031 and heartbeat-loss rules once change-window baselines are clean. Shipping absence-of-signal detection before that baseline exists floods the queue and trains analysts to ignore it. IOC lists for POORTRY and the LOLDrivers project are in the public loldrivers[.]io catalog.

item.title: Fake Web3 Accelerator Uses npm Packages to Spread Malware and Hijack AI Agent Traffic
item.description:
Fake Web3 "accelerator" REF8801 targets crypto founders with malicious npm packages delivering a Windows infostealer, a macOS backdoor, and AI agent hijacking via MCP server abuse.
Key findings:
- The operation impersonates a venture capital accelerator called Apex Accelerator (npm user "apexaccelerator," GitHub "apexaccs," domains apexaccs[.]org and apexfdn[.]xyz), approaching cryptocurrency wallet developers and market intelligence builders on X with offers of $235,000 investments and requests to run their "due diligence" tool. Elastic Security Labs tracks this as REF8801. The group built credibility by appearing at TOKEN2049 in Singapore 🇸🇬. Neither npm package ([@]apexacc/cli or [@]apexacc/audit) delivers the promised functionality: the 18 security tools generate fabricated findings and the AI advisor returns nonsense assessments.
- The Windows infection chain is multi-stage and deliberately evasive. An HTTP POST to vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf kicks off a Base64-encoded PowerShell command that pulls drop.ps1 from 0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService, which downloads bludness.exe from ehegisnightmare[.]icu. A PyInstaller loader checks for admin rights, attempts UAC bypass via UACME's ucmDebugObjectMethod() if not elevated, and writes exegis.exe to %TEMP%. A Golang stage then patches AMSI and ETW and unhooks ntdll.dll before reflectively loading shellcode that harvests credentials, session cookies, clipboard content, Wi-Fi profiles, screenshots, browser data (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Yandex) including Chrome app-bound encryption bypass, crypto wallets, messenger clients, VPN configs, FTP and remote-access tools, and game clients. Everything exfiltrates over Telegram.
- The macOS chain downloads a bash script that pulls a GZIP archive from verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/ as package.tar.gz, drops a backdoor called CloudSyncD, phishes the victim's login password with a fake system authorization prompt, and uses it to sudo-launch an embedded payload. That payload performs host discovery, collects hardware and OS details, beacons to ccmihr[.]com for tasking, and can download and run additional payloads. CloudSyncD was first documented by Jamf Threat Labs in late September 2026 spreading via a fake Zoom installer, and shows a clear trend toward native macOS implementations that minimize on-disk writes.
- Beyond credential theft, both packages redirect OpenRouter LLM traffic to an attacker-controlled API endpoint and register a rogue MCP server in the victim's AI agent configuration. This gives the attacker access to every prompt, conversation turn, code snippet, and tool output the agent sends, and lets the attacker inject instructions and fabricated tool definitions back into the agent's prompt, shaping its subsequent actions. This is not a theoretical supply-chain risk: it is a running interception proxy for AI developer workflows.
- The campaign has been active since at least April 2026. SafeDep documented an earlier wave in late July 2026 covering three related packages: [@]apexfdn/apex, [@]copilot-mcp/apex, and [@]apexfdn/copilot-mcp, distributing Atomic Stealer (AMOS) on macOS. REF8801 is iterating tradecraft across waves, rotating package names while keeping the same social engineering premise and infrastructure pattern.
Practitioner takeaway: if you support developers in Web3 or AI agent tooling, hunt npm install history and agent configuration files for [@]apexacc or [@]apexfdn namespaced packages. Check MCP server registrations in agent configs for entries pointing to unexpected external hosts. On Windows, look for exegis.exe or updater_loader.exe in %TEMP%, PowerShell reaching 0auth-chromium[.]com or ehegisnightmare[.]icu, and evidence of ntdll.dll unhooking or AMSI patch. On macOS, look for package.tar.gz in temp directories, fake sudo password prompts, and outbound connections to ccmihr[.]com. IOCs and full technical detail are in the Elastic Security Labs report.

item.title: Big Fish: OpenBSD Root Exploit Chains a 37-Year-Old BSD Bug With a Kernel Flaw
item.description:
A public exploit chains a 37-year-old signed integer overflow with a kernel use-after-free on OpenBSD 7.9, bypassing KARL, SMAP, and SMEP to reach root without any info-leak primitive.
Key findings:
- The root cause is shm_nattch, a shared memory attachment counter defined as a signed 16-bit integer (max 32,767) in BSD source code in 1988 and inherited by OpenBSD unchanged. An attacker maps 127 shared memory segments and forks 259 processes to wrap the counter to a negative value, triggering a use-after-free through a race condition won by calling IPC_RMID in one process while a helper simultaneously attaches a size-confused segment. No CVE has been assigned to either flaw as of publication.
- The second flaw extends the first: the corrupted counter enables an out-of-bounds write that overwrites multicast membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting counter updates modify page table entries, promoting user memory to supervisor-level access. This is how SMAP and SMEP fall, not through a direct hardware attack but by corrupting the kernel's internal memory accounting.
- KARL rerandomizes kernel binary layout at boot, but the kernel's own allocators lack base address randomization. Early boot allocations, including function pointers in lo0 and enc0 interface ioctl handlers, land at the same addresses on every reboot on the same hardware. The exploit uses sysctl kernel memory allocation metrics from userland to track live heap allocations and time the race, targeting those predictable addresses without needing a separate info-leak.
- OpenBSD patched both issues before the public write-up: the integer overflow in errata 018 (September 14) and the use-after-free in errata 026 (September 30), both available via syspatch across all architectures. Calif reports no evidence of in-the-wild exploitation. The same research also identified 21 related issues reported to FreeBSD.
- The report recommends four hardening improvements OpenBSD currently lacks: safe-unlinking for kernel linked lists (already present in FreeBSD and NetBSD), boot-time randomization of the page table self-referential mapping, base address randomization for the kernel allocator, and array bounds checks in release builds.
Practitioner takeaway: if you run OpenBSD 7.9 and have not applied errata 018 and 026 via syspatch, do it now. The full exploit and write-up are public. For defenders on shared or multi-tenant OpenBSD systems, local access is all the prerequisite an attacker needs. The Calif write-up details the heap shaping technique, the sysctl side channel used for allocation tracking, and the specific ioctl handler structures targeted, giving you the primitives to understand what post-exploitation on a compromised host would look like.

item.title: Attackers Abuse Stolen ConnectWise Application Credentials to Target Microsoft 365
item.description:
Stolen ConnectWise application credentials granted attackers OAuth-level access to Microsoft 365 tenants, with roughly 300 successful sign-ins recorded and a manual second wave targeting policy, national security, trade, and critical minerals sectors.
Key details:
- Attackers obtained seven ConnectWise application identities, likely before October 13, and used them to request access tokens from Microsoft Entra ID without ever touching customer passwords. Because ConnectWise's apps already held delegated permissions to customer tenants, valid app credentials were all the attackers needed. Depending on the permissions scoped to each application, reachable data included mailboxes, SharePoint documents, Teams messages, and directory data.
- Of roughly 1,000 Entra tenants that recorded sign-in activity from 144.172.64[.]128, approximately 300 sign-ins succeeded. A second, manually driven wave on October 15 at around 14:20 UTC specifically targeted 16 tenants in policy, national security, trade, and critical minerals sectors, hitting Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and Office 365 Management APIs in rapid succession. All 16 second-wave attempts failed, but the deliberate sector targeting is significant threat-intel context.
- Revoking the compromised ConnectWise credentials stops new authentication but does not undo what already happened inside a tenant. Huntress documented the persistence risk clearly: an attacker who entered via the stolen app credential could add a client secret to a different trusted application already registered in that tenant, create a net-new application and grant it permissions, assign directory roles including Global Administrator, reset user passwords and authentication methods, or modify Conditional Access policies. Every one of those actions survives the vendor credential revocation and provides an independent path back in.
- ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly SkyKick, remains suspended as of the report. Scheduled backups are not running and restoration is unavailable. The archives themselves are described as encrypted, isolated, and preserved with no evidence of access, but the operational outage creates real recovery risk for organizations dependent on the service.
Practitioner takeaway: Before running any containment steps, preserve Entra sign-in logs and unified audit logs, because remediation actions can overwrite the evidence baseline. Then audit every affected tenant, including dormant SkyKick-connected tenants, for sign-in activity from 144.172.64[.]128 starting October 13. Work through the full persistence checklist: application credentials and registered app secrets, federation trusts, directory role assignments, OAuth consent grants, recent Conditional Access policy changes, mailbox forwarding rules, and delegated mailbox access. IOCs and the full advisory are available in the ConnectWise alert and the Huntress report.

item.title: 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Bug Lets Attackers Take Over Routers Without a Password
item.description:
A 16-year-old unauthenticated RCE flaw in Broadcom's 802.11 WPS implementation affects over 1.5 million ISP-provided routers in Belgium 🇧🇪 alone, with no CVE assigned and no patch for eCos-based platforms by design.
Key findings:
- The flaw lives in the WPS EAP reassembly code inside Broadcom's proprietary 802.11 SDK, present since at least 2010. An attacker within Wi-Fi range can trigger it without knowing the network key or completing WPS enrollment, delivering controlled information disclosure and arbitrary code execution. No user interaction required. Broadcom shipped an incomplete, silent fix in 2018, then told OEMs to migrate to hostapd instead of patching their own code.
- Platform status matters for triage. eCos-based chipsets (BCM3380, BCM3383, BCM33834) are permanently unpatched by design, a forever day with no remediation path. Linux-based chipsets (BCM3390, BCM65xx, BCM68xx) remain exposed unless individual OEMs choose to act. Confirmed vulnerable devices include the Orange Belgium 🇧🇪 ASKEY TCG3000 and the Proximus Sagemcom F@st/BBOX3V+, both demonstrated with working exploits.
- The demonstrated exploit chain is concrete and severe. Researcher Quentin Kaiser extracted the Wi-Fi PSK directly from the router's NVRAM and exfiltrated it over Wi-Fi frames. In a second demonstration he opened a reverse shell using only Wi-Fi frames, no internet-accessible C2 server required. Both attacks ran without authentication. Laboratory antenna proximity in the videos was a setup convenience, not an attack requirement.
- Disclosure failed completely. Kaiser reported to Broadcom in July 2026. Broadcom said a patch existed and directed him to tell affected OEMs to contact Broadcom themselves. The company refused to assign a CVE and declined to share its internal notification. CERT/CC opened and closed the case the same day after confirming Broadcom had no intention of assigning a CVE. As of October 15, 2026, no affected Belgian 🇧🇪 devices had received a patch.
- Scope is large and still unmapped. Kaiser's estimate using Belgian 🇧🇪 telecom market data puts exposure at roughly 850,000 Proximus devices, 500,000 VOO legacy units, and 210,000 Orange Belgium 🇧🇪 gateways, over 1.5 million in one small country. Broadcom chipsets appear across dozens of vendors and hundreds of products globally. Telenet exposure via Sagemcom devices is unconfirmed. Kaiser is publishing a fingerprinting script and a YARA rule to help map the full scope.
Takeaway: ISP-provided routers are a near-invisible blind spot in most enterprise and home network monitoring. If your environment includes Broadcom BCM3380, BCM3383, BCM33834, BCM3390, BCM65xx, or BCM68xx-based gateways, assume no patch is coming for eCos variants. The fingerprinting script and YARA rule Kaiser is publishing are the starting point for scoping exposure. For incident responders, a compromised gateway at this layer intercepts traffic silently with no footprint on endpoint telemetry. Threat models for high-value targets in range-relevant environments (hotels, shared office buildings, residential surveillance scenarios) should account for Wi-Fi-range RCE requiring zero credentials. Check firmware versions against affected chipsets and escalate to ISPs where OEM action is the only remediation path.

item.title: Heartbreaker 💔
item.description:
Previously undetected macOS ransomware "Heartbreaker" carries its own Rust source code and attempts metamorphic self-rebuilding via the native Cargo toolchain, yet remains catchable through entropy-based behavioral detection.
Key findings:
- Heartbreaker is an ad hoc-signed ARM64 Mach-O binary written in Rust, first uploaded to VirusTotal in May 2025 and still undetected by all AV engines as of this writing. It recursively targets files under ~/Downloads, truncating and overwriting each in place before appending the .heartbreaker extension, then drops a ransom note at ~/Desktop/README.txt. Crucially, it encrypts every file with AES-GCM using a single hard-coded key (g_w:D2Xq6Yxez-5{#3mfd=VcB.Qhsub) and stores the 12-byte nonce at the head of each encrypted file (layout: 12-byte nonce || ciphertext || 16-byte GCM tag), meaning full file recovery without ransom payment is possible using that static key.
- Persistence is established via a LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist with RunAtLoad set to true, pointing back to the running Heartbreaker binary. The rationale is to re-run on subsequent logins and encrypt any new or restored files added to ~/Downloads. The persistence call is fire-and-forget: a failure does not halt encryption.
- The metamorphic component is the most forensically interesting element. Using Rust's include_str! macro, Heartbreaker embeds its own main[.]rs and build[.]rs directly in the compiled Mach-O. After displaying the ransom window, it passes those embedded sources to mimicore::morph(), which strips previously generated junk, randomizes identifiers, inserts 15 new junk functions, reconstructs a Cargo.toml, and calls cargo build --release. A successful build replaces the on-disk binary with the recompiled version, which itself embeds the newly transformed source. Each generation produces a different hash and Mach-O UUID. In practice the scheme is fragile: the Cargo.toml references the now-unavailable mimicore repository, so rebuilding fails unless the dependency is already cached, and the Rust install-and-compile workflow is exceptionally noisy on disk and in process telemetry.
- Apple's Endpoint Security framework is what makes behavioral detection tractable here. item.content:encoded:
Previously undetected macOS ransomware "Heartbreaker" carries its own Rust source code and attempts metamorphic self-rebuilding via the native Cargo toolchain, yet remains catchable through entropy-based behavioral detection.

Key findings:

- Heartbreaker is an ad hoc-signed ARM64 Mach-O binary written in Rust, first uploaded to VirusTotal in May 2025 and still undetected by all AV engines as of this writing. It recursively targets files under ~/Downloads, truncating and overwriting each in place before appending the .heartbreaker extension, then drops a ransom note at ~/Desktop/README.txt. Crucially, it encrypts every file with AES-GCM using a single hard-coded key (g_w:D2Xq6Yxez-5{#3mfd=VcB.Qhsub) and stores the 12-byte nonce at the head of each encrypted file (layout: 12-byte nonce || ciphertext || 16-byte GCM tag), meaning full file recovery without ransom payment is possible using that static key.

- Persistence is established via a LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist with RunAtLoad set to true, pointing back to the running Heartbreaker binary. The rationale is to re-run on subsequent logins and encrypt any new or restored files added to ~/Downloads. The persistence call is fire-and-forget: a failure does not halt encryption.

- The metamorphic component is the most forensically interesting element. Using Rust's include_str! macro, Heartbreaker embeds its own main[.]rs and build[.]rs directly in the compiled Mach-O. After displaying the ransom window, it passes those embedded sources to mimicore::morph(), which strips previously generated junk, randomizes identifiers, inserts 15 new junk functions, reconstructs a Cargo.toml, and calls cargo build --release. A successful build replaces the on-disk binary with the recompiled version, which itself embeds the newly transformed source. Each generation produces a different hash and Mach-O UUID. In practice the scheme is fragile: the Cargo.toml references the now-unavailable mimicore repository, so rebuilding fails unless the dependency is already cached, and the Rust install-and-compile workflow is exceptionally noisy on disk and in process telemetry.

- Apple's Endpoint Security framework is what makes behavioral detection tractable here. RansomWhere? subscribes to modified-file close events, catching Heartbreaker's in-place truncate-and-overwrite pattern (not just new-file creation). When an untrusted process rapidly writes high-entropy data to multiple files, the tool suspends the process and alerts the user, detecting Heartbreaker without any sample-specific signature. The metamorphic rebuild is irrelevant to this logic: the behavior required to encrypt files cannot be removed without removing the ransomware's purpose.

- Documented evasion limits and artifact opportunities worth noting: the self-rebuild generates substantial process and filesystem noise (cargo invocations, temporary build directories, binary replacement on disk), the LaunchAgent plist at com[.]network.startup.plist is a persistent artifact, and the static AES-GCM key embedded in every build generation means any recovered sample yields a universal decryptor. item.title: Orphaned VBA Projects Inside DWG Files: YARA Rule, (Sun, Oct 18th)
item.description:
Orphaned VBA projects embedded inside AutoCAD DWG files are a low-detection hiding spot for malicious macros, and a YARA rule now makes retrohunting viable.
Key findings:
- The technique embeds an OLE2 Compound Document (the VBA project container) inside a DWG file alongside the AutoCAD version header "AC10" at offset 0, creating what the author calls an orphaned VBA project. The DWG structure signals no embedded object at offset 0x24 (the value equals 0), yet the OLE2 magic bytes D0 CF 11 E0 A1 B1 1A E1 and a "[Host Extender Info]" string are both present, exposing the hidden payload.
- The YARA rule targets exactly this combination: the AC10 magic at offset 0, a null uint32 at 0x24, the OLE2 header bytes anywhere in the file, and the ASCII string "[Host Extender Info]". Those four conditions together fingerprint the anomaly without matching clean DWG files or standard OLE documents.
- A VirusTotal retrohunt using this rule returned only 2 hits, suggesting the technique is rare in the wild right now, which cuts both ways. It means defenders who deploy this rule will generate almost no noise, but it also means the few files that do match deserve close scrutiny.
- AutoCAD's VBA engine can execute macro code embedded this way, making DWG files a plausible delivery vehicle for engineering and OT environments where CAD files are routine and may bypass standard Office-macro controls. The "orphaned" framing matters: the VBA project is not properly linked in the DWG structure, which is why conventional parsers and most AV engines miss it.
Practitioners working in environments that handle AutoCAD files, especially ICS/OT shops, manufacturing, or architecture firms, should add this rule to their retrohunt rotation. Deploy it against your mail gateway archives, file share snapshots, and any DWG files received from external parties. The rule and all four conditions are in the SANS ISC diary by Didier Stevens; grab it directly from that post. Any match in your environment is anomalous by definition given the near-zero baseline on VirusTotal.

item.title: ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup After Attackers Compromise Microsoft 365 Tenants
item.description:
ConnectWise application identity compromise lets attackers authenticate directly into Microsoft 365 tenants as trusted apps, hitting policy, national security, and critical mineral sector targets across roughly 300 confirmed tenant sign-ins.
Key findings:
- Seven ConnectWise application identities were stolen, including Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519), Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb), MS Graph (0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827), Partner Center (412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e), and Cloud Management (2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83). ConnectWise disabled these on October 17 at 07:00 UTC, but previously issued access tokens may remain valid until they expire. The Cloud Management apps for Exchange, Teams, and SharePoint had not been disabled as of late Saturday, per Huntress, leaving a live abuse path.
- The attacker's playbook after obtaining an application credential was to authenticate as the application itself against Microsoft Entra ID, then escalate by adding the application to the Global Administrator role, planting new client secrets on other trusted applications, and creating new app registrations with granted permissions. Each planted secret is an independent persistence mechanism that survives revocation of the original stolen credential. Incident responders must treat every app registration and service principal touched during the window as potentially backdoored, not just the seven named ConnectWise identities.
- Huntress tracked malicious sign-ins from 144.172.64[.]128 beginning around October 13. The last observed sign-in from that IP on the original target set was October 15 at 08:45 UTC, with manual activity continuing until approximately 14:20 UTC. A second, targeted wave hit 16 tenants in the policy, national security, trade, and critical mineral sectors on October 15, first sweeping for Graph tokens from the SkyKick app (09:25 to 12:35 UTC), then manually targeting Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and the Office 365 Management APIs (13:54 to 14:20 UTC). Huntress confirmed abuse of the Teams app in at least one tenant.
- Across nearly 1,000 Entra tenants showing sign-in activity from that IP, approximately 300 sign-ins succeeded. In some cases, the absence of a service principal in the tenant blocked the attacker from gaining further access, which underscores that service principal provisioning is itself an attack surface worth auditing. ConnectWise identified the issue October 14 through internal monitoring; the credential-exposure mechanism remains under investigation.
Practitioner takeaway: Preserve Entra sign-in logs and audit logs before any containment action. Review all sign-in activity from 144.172.64[.]128 from October 13 onward. Hunt for new or modified app registrations, added client secrets, changes to directory role membership, new federation trusts, consent grants, and delegated mailbox access created during that window. Check for unauthorized mailbox forwarding rules and transport rules that could persist after credential revocation. Do not limit scope to the seven named ConnectWise identities: any app the attacker could reach with Global Administrator rights is a candidate for a planted secret. IOCs and detailed response guidance are in the Huntress report.

item.title: Frozen Privilege: Remote Code Execution in Snowflake-Managed PostgreSQL
item.description:
A five-link privilege chain turned a non-superuser Snowflake Postgres role into full OS-level RCE, bypassing every published mitigation without disabling a single one. Snowflake remediated server-side; no customer action required, but the pattern recurs across managed PostgreSQL.
Key findings:
- The chain starts from snowflake_admin, a non-superuser role whose only attribute was CREATEROLE. Since PostgreSQL 14, CREATEROLE alone lets a role self-grant predefined pg_* system roles, including pg_read_all_data and pg_write_all_data, without superuser involvement. That single attribute was the entire foothold, and it is widely underestimated as a privilege-escalation primitive.
- With pg_write_all_data in hand, the chain wrote directly to the cron.job table, rewriting a scheduled job's username to "postgres". Because pg_cron executes jobs over the local socket as any user with no password, the scheduler fired a SECURITY DEFINER backdoor function as superuser, elevating the attacker's role to snowflake_superuser without ever calling ALTER ROLE ... SUPERUSER, which Snowflake blocks.
- Snowflake had blocked the standard SQL-to-OS paths: COPY TO PROGRAM, ALTER SYSTEM, pg_read_file(), and pg_read_server_files. The bypass used LANGUAGE internal to rebind the compiled C symbols still present in the PostgreSQL binary under new SQL names, reconstructing lo_export for arbitrary file write and pg_read_file for arbitrary file read. A catalog-level blocklist does not remove the underlying capability; it removes one door handle while the compiled symbol remains.
- Arbitrary file write via the rebound lo_export was aimed at postgresql[.]auto.conf, injecting a shell command into archive_command. PostgreSQL runs archive_command through /bin/sh -c as the postgres OS user on every completed WAL segment, making it the cleanest command sink in the engine. The result was OS-level RCE as uid=26. Pre-RCE file reads pulled Snowflake's internal tenant mTLS private key and certificate and plaintext AWS STS credentials from the host.
- Post-exploitation impact extends well beyond SQL: on-disk heap file edits alter table contents with no SQL statement recorded and no actor attribution, WAL segment modification breaks point-in-time recovery and replication, and pg_control or clog corruption can prevent the cluster from starting. A persisted SECURITY DEFINER function survives credential rotation entirely, turning a one-time credential compromise into a durable foothold.
Practitioner takeaway: if you operate PostgreSQL, treat CREATEROLE as near-superuser and revoke it from every application and service-account role. Audit cron.job for unexpected username values and review SECURITY DEFINER functions for anything not created by the platform. Restrict LANGUAGE internal and LANGUAGE c function creation to platform roles only, because removing a SQL name does not remove the compiled symbol. Make postgresql[.]auto.conf immutable or block lo_export writes to the data directory. For Snowflake Postgres specifically, replace static passwords with short-lived Snowflake-issued tokens, apply network policies or PrivateLink, and alert on GRANT statements touching CREATEROLE, pg_read_all_data, pg_write_all_data, or system role membership. The full chain and bypass table are in the Varonis report.

item.title: ConnectWise SkyKick Breach: How to Check Your Microsoft 365 Tenant
item.description:
Active supply chain attack: a compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential was used to access Microsoft 365 customer tenants between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC on October 15, 2026, with Huntress confirming unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants.
Key details:
- The attacker used the ConnectWise Cloud Backup service principal credential (app ID: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, owned by ConnectWise tenant 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7) to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants. MFA does not apply to application sign-ins, so the attacker inherited whatever permissions customers had already granted the app, likely including Directory.ReadWrite.All, giving access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and directory data with no user interaction or prompt.
- The attacker's movement pattern was seconds apart per tenant, consistent with an automated script working through a target list. The source IP is 144.172.64[.]128, a hosting provider address. Six ConnectWise and Cloud Management app IDs are implicated beyond the primary Cloud Backup app, all owned by the same ConnectWise organization ID.
- In at least one tenant, a second ConnectWise application granted itself Global Administrator and added new client secrets to two other trusted applications. This creates persistence paths that survive a credential reset on the original compromised app: even after the primary entry point is closed, attacker-added secrets on other service principals remain valid.
- Tokens issued before an app is disabled can remain valid for up to 90 minutes. Disabling the app stops new authentications but does not immediately invalidate already-issued tokens, meaning the window for lateral movement inside a tenant extends past the moment you pull the plug.
Immediate steps: disable app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae in Entra admin center now, then review Entra sign-in logs filtering on all six ConnectWise app IDs and source IP 144.172.64[.]128. Critically, audit every application in your tenant for client secrets or credentials added since October 13, not just the ConnectWise apps, because the persistence technique involves adding secrets to other trusted apps. The SpecterOps report includes two BloodHound Cypher queries to map outbound control from the ConnectWise service principal and shortest paths to Tier Zero assets: run those against your AzureHound-collected data to understand your blast radius before deciding what else to revoke.

- In at least one tenant, a second ConnectWise application granted itself Global Administrator and added new client secrets to two other trusted applications. This creates persistence paths that survive a credential reset on the original compromised app: even after the primary entry point is closed, attacker-added secrets on other service principals remain valid.

- Tokens issued before an app is disabled can remain valid for up to 90 minutes. Disabling the app stops new authentications but does not immediately invalidate already-issued tokens, meaning the window for lateral movement inside a tenant extends past the moment you pull the plug.

Immediate steps: disable app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae in Entra admin center now, then review Entra sign-in logs filtering on all six ConnectWise app IDs and source IP 144.172.64[.]128. Critically, audit every application in your tenant for client secrets or credentials added since October 13, not just the ConnectWise apps, because the persistence technique involves adding secrets to other trusted apps. The SpecterOps report includes two BloodHound Cypher queries to map outbound control from the ConnectWise service principal and shortest paths to Tier Zero assets: run those against your AzureHound-collected data to understand your blast radius before deciding what else to revoke.

item.title: Hackers breach Microsoft 365 tenants via ConnectWise supply-chain attack
item.description:
Active supply-chain attack against ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromised Microsoft 365 service principals across at least 162 tenants, with confirmed persistence, credential addition, and Graph API reconnaissance observed by mid-October 2026.
Key findings:
- The attacker authenticated directly to Microsoft 365 as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application (app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae) using the application's own secret, bypassing MFA entirely because no user login was involved. Scripted sign-in attempts began as early as October 13 and 14, using the user agent curl/7.88.1, followed by python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31, and python-requests/2.34.2. All malicious authentication traced back to a single IP: 144.172.64[.]128.
- Because the backup service principal already held broad pre-granted permissions including Directory.ReadWrite.All, the attacker immediately had the technical ability to read and write mail, OneDrive and SharePoint files, and Teams chats across every affected tenant without needing to escalate privileges from scratch.
- On nearly 50 monitored tenants, Huntress observed ConnectWise Cloud Management service principals assigning themselves the Exchange Administrator directory role. In at least one tenant, the Cloud Management MS Teams app (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) granted itself Global Administrator, then added credentials to an MSP management tool and to Huntress's own application, completing a persistence step in roughly five minutes.
- Microsoft confirmed persistence via backdoor after successful service principal authentication, followed by Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials. ConnectWise shutting down application access does not revoke already-planted credentials or invalidate existing application tokens: those tokens remain live until natural expiration, and revoking user sessions has no effect on application-based access.
- The seven implicated application IDs span the full ConnectWise Cloud Management suite: Cloud Backup (506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), Cloud Management (2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83), MS Teams (24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640), Exchange Online (b78f6a77-d4e5-46fb-87e5-d1648bd02519), MS Graph (0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827), Partner Center (412dcf96-176d-4b3a-a1b0-4981ad66971e), and SharePoint Online (b2b55f5b-7758-4719-8d8f-88ae172e6bdb). Older tenants may list these under the SkyKick Cloud Manager name.
Practitioner takeaway: In Entra ID, pull service principal sign-in logs filtered by each of the seven application IDs above and flag any authentication from 144.172.64[.]128 or bearing those user agent strings. Audit secrets and certificates added to all seven applications since October 13 and remove unauthorized entries immediately: shutdown does not clean up planted credentials. Review directory role assignment events for unexpected Exchange Administrator or Global Administrator grants from these principals, and check for Microsoft Graph API calls that followed authentication, particularly credential-addition operations. Disabling the applications stops new token issuance, but hunt for any access tokens still in use until expiry.

item.title: Investigation: Unauthorized Access Through the ConnectWise Cloud Backup Microsoft 365 App
item.description:
A stolen OAuth client secret for the ConnectWise Cloud Backup Microsoft 365 app (formerly SkyKick) gave an attacker app-only access to mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams across multiple tenants on October 15, 2026, with no MFA or Conditional Access in the path.
Key findings:
- The attack abused the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow. The actor presented the app's stolen client secret directly to Microsoft Entra ID, which issued app-only access tokens for Microsoft Graph in every consenting tenant, one token per tenant, between 07:11 and 08:47 UTC on October 15. No user interaction was required, so MFA and user-scoped Conditional Access policies offered no protection. The app ID is 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, published from ConnectWise S-K LLC tenant 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7. A single stolen vendor-held credential unlocks every tenant that has ever consented.
- The sweep was automated and loud once you know where to look. All requests came from a single IPv4 address, 144.172.64[.]128, using user agents Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31, in strictly ascending tenant-GUID order, roughly 1-6 minutes apart. Legitimate backup traffic authenticates from Microsoft internal fd00:: IPv6 ranges. The GUID crawl pattern, the Python user agent, and the VPS source IP together make this trivially distinguishable from a real backup job in the Service principal sign-ins log, but only if you are looking there, not the User sign-ins tab.
- Data exposure scope is real but partially invisible. The app's pre-granted permissions cover tenant-wide read/write to mail and attachments via Exchange Web Services, OneDrive and SharePoint files, and Teams chats. For tenants without an active backup subscription, only a token issuance was confirmed, consistent with reconnaissance. For tenants with an active subscription, read activity exists in the audit log but cannot be attributed to the actor because both the actor and the legitimate service share the same application identity. Per-request source IPs live in MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs, which were not enabled for these tenants, leaving a visibility gap that cannot be closed retroactively.
- No persistence was established in directory terms. Todyl found no new secrets, app registrations, consent grants, or role assignments made by the backup app in any tenant. The activity was sign-in only, which means the attacker is not currently burrowed into Entra, but the token exposure window is up to 90 minutes after the sign-in, and any tenant where the app remains enabled stays exposed until ConnectWise rotates the credential. Revoking user sessions has no effect on app-only tokens.
- Containment requires two parallel actions. In Entra, open Enterprise applications, filter All applications, search by app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, and set "Enabled for users to sign-in?" to No. This blocks new token issuance immediately. Do not delete the app yet: disabling preserves the audit trail and allows re-enabling without a new consent workflow. Then disable every other SkyKick/ConnectWise app in the same publisher tenant that you do not actively use. The second required action is vendor-side: only ConnectWise can rotate the client secret. ConnectWise's October 16 advisory acknowledged unauthorized access attempts but had not confirmed credential rotation as of that publication.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt in the Service principal sign-ins tab in Entra, not User sign-ins, filtered on app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, back to October 1 or your retention limit. Flag 144.172.64[.]128, user agents Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31, and any non-Microsoft IP. In the unified audit log, look for mail, file, and Teams read events where ClientAppId matches. In the directory audit log, check for consent grants, role assignments, and new credentials made by any SkyKick/ConnectWise app. If you are on Entra ID Free with 7-day retention, export logs now. Enable MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs going forward: without them you cannot separate legitimate backup reads from attacker reads when they share the same app identity.

item.title: MALFEX npm Package 'imgdecode' Hides Shellcode Loader in Windows Native Addon
item.description:
MALFEX supply chain campaign evolves fast: npm package "imgdecode" buries a compiled DLL shellcode loader inside a Windows native Node.js addon, injecting into dllhost.exe and delivering a full-featured RAT and stealer.
Key findings:
- The MALFEX campaign has run since August 6, 2023 across five npm publisher handles (malfexkkj, malfex_user, malfexteste2, malfexteste3, malfexteste4). The latest package, imgdecode (publisher: malfexteste8, now at version 1.0.3, 979 downloads), follows a clear operator playbook: when npm removes a package, replacements appear within hours. imgdecode 1.0.3 published October 11, 2026 is now fully self-contained and requires no other MALFEX package to execute.
- The infection chain for imgdecode works like this: require('imgdecode') loads a 64-bit MSVC DLL as a native Node.js addon. The DLL checks for developer terminals, then fetches banner.jpg from the GitHub repo cavecrew/proj, decrypts the embedded payload using the key "nif-runtime-2027," and injects the result into a spawned dllhost.exe process. A kill switch is baked in: if the decrypted bytes match a JPEG or PNG header, the loader stops, letting the operator serve a benign image to disable delivery on demand.
- The earlier stealer chain (cdn-img-fetch, img-to-native, native-runner) dropped a Go executable at %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\node_runtime_helper.exe using decryption key "malfexteam2027," then pulled a stealer binary called "movinlike" (setup.exe) from 104.234.65[.]75:700. A .env file inside the Node.js payload contains the C2 address 104.234.65[.]75:7007 and a MALFEX license key, suggesting a malware-as-a-service builder backend. Three of the eight identified packages delivered Overlord RAT.
- The stealer component (movinlike) runs anti-analysis checks for VMs, sandboxes, Process Monitor, and Wireshark before targeting seed phrase files, .kdbx, .pem, .ppk, and .env files, Chromium browser data, Discord, Telegram, cryptocurrency wallets, and gaming platforms (Steam, Epic Games, Riot, Battle[.]net, Minecraft, Ubisoft). Persistence lands via a Registry Run key and a scheduled task named "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateService," a name chosen to blend with legitimate Edge updater tasks.
- The WebSocket C2 connection at 104.234.65[.]75:7007 supports shell execution, file transfer, process control, clipboard access, screenshots, and mouse/keyboard input, making this a full remote access capability, not just exfiltration.
Practitioner takeaway: If any of these packages (imgdecode, imgbundle, runhelper, cdn-img-fetch, img-to-native, native-runner) appear in a project's package.json or node_modules, treat the host as compromised. Hunt for %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\node_runtime_helper.exe, a scheduled task named "MicrosoftEdgeUpdateService," and dllhost.exe processes with unusual parent processes or outbound connections to 104.234.65[.]75. Check Registry Run keys for persistence entries added around the package install date. Rotate all credentials, API keys, and .env secrets stored on the system, and treat any seed phrases as burned. IOCs and full technical detail are in the SafeDep report.

item.title: Two Hawks in a Pod: one Android RAT behind a flock of fake Japanese brands
item.description:
A single Android RAT sits behind 64 samples impersonating Japanese 🇯🇵 finance brands, tax portals, and romance apps, all phoning home to hawk-branded control panels and built for financial fraud.
Key findings:
- The dropper (reference sample SHA256: 24e58e12c24180abf800f142b83348b318f60894f94571a68eea98481abd84f0, package com.nova.core.high) is packed with a trivially reversible libsa XOR stub: a plaintext 32-byte key (AK) and asset name (AN) sit in the Sa application class, and hand-XORing the asset produces the inner dex with all config constants in the clear. That inner dex holds a single config class Cf with the C2 (S1), an AES-256 key (K1), the payload asset name (N1), and the dropped RAT package name com[.]open.stone[.]love. A second packer, the open-source maoabc/nmmp VM (libnmmp[.]so, libnmmvm[.]so), is used on another set of droppers where the config is harder to extract but the VM's instruction set is Android's own, only the 256-opcode table is reshuffled per build.
- The RAT (com[.]open.stone[.]love) connects over WebSocket wss://<host>/w?d=<deviceId>, with every message authenticated by a per-device BouncyCastle Ed25519 keypair (stored in shared prefs rt_kp, keys k_priv and k_pub), a timestamped HMAC, and a pinned TLS certificate, all native-only via libnauth[.]so with the C2 host XOR-0xC3 obfuscated inside it. On device, flag any non-developer app whose native libraries include libspake2[.]so and libdxs[.]so performing ADB pairing, or any app self-granting WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS. item.title: ConnectWise (SkyKick) Vendor Credentials Abused in M365 Attacks
item.description:
ConnectWise (SkyKick) vendor credentials compromised, granting attackers Microsoft Graph tokens across 162 confirmed M365 tenants. MSP environments face compounding risk as broad backup permissions enable bulk data access with minimal audit trail.
Key findings:
- The attacker obtained the ConnectWise Cloud Backup service principal credential (App ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae) from the vendor's own tenant (owner tenant ID 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7), then replayed it against every customer tenant where the app is consented. Authentication came from 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting) between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC on October 15. Tenants were hit in sorted GUID order, seconds apart, consistent with a script working from a list. This is a supply-chain credential abuse scenario: the customer did nothing wrong, and nothing on their side could have prevented the initial sign-in.
- In one tenant, the ConnectWise Cloud Management for MS Teams app (App ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) assigned itself Global Administrator at 03:44 UTC, then a Python-urllib/3.12 User-Agent process modified two other applications, adding client secrets expiring in 2028 to an MSP management app and to the Huntress Security Platform app. This is T1098.001 (Additional Cloud Credentials) and T1098.003 (Additional Cloud Roles). The entire sequence took roughly five minutes. Because app-only sign-ins bypass MFA entirely, those planted secrets give the attacker durable, user-independent access until they are explicitly removed.
- The audit trail is partial by design. Microsoft's Entra audit log records Add member to role, Update application, and Add service principal credentials events, but app-only actions carry no source IP. Directory reads through Microsoft Graph leave no audit trail at all, so confirmed token issuance does not rule out bulk mailbox, OneDrive, SharePoint, or Teams data access. The absence of visible read activity is not evidence of absence. Scope today: 162 confirmed tenants, with reconnaissance via password spray observed against four law firm tenants on October 13 to 14 using curl/7.88.1 from the same IP.
- The ATT&CK mapping the report gives: T1078.004 (Valid Cloud Accounts) for use of the vendor credential, T1098.003 (Additional Cloud Roles) for self-assigned administrator roles, and T1098.001 (Additional Cloud Credentials) for secrets added to other applications. The User-Agent pattern is a useful distinguisher: legitimate ConnectWise Cloud Management and Partner Center apps use kiota-dotnet for Graph calls; the malicious credential additions used Python-urllib/3.12, and the password spray used curl/7.88.1. No single agent is conclusive, but the combination with the acting application and operation is the signal.
- MSP exposure is the force multiplier. Management applications consented into many customer tenants mean a credential planted in one MSP tenant can propagate outward. The report has not confirmed lateral movement across MSP customers but flags it as the primary structural risk.
Practitioner takeaway: In Entra admin center, go to Monitoring, Service principal sign-ins, filter on App ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae, and look for 144.172.64[.]128 or any non-Azure egress IP. Then sweep all Enterprise applications and App registrations for client secrets or certificates added since October 13 that you did not create, paying special attention to App IDs 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640, 2399d300-6fca-4e6a-a686-399fefe75b83, and the full list in the report. Disable, do not delete, any ConnectWise or SkyKick service principal until ConnectWise confirms credential rotation. Hunt Entra audit logs for Add member to role and Add service principal credentials events where the initiating application is a ConnectWise or SkyKick principal. IOCs are in the report.

item.title: Hackers Use Compromised ConnectWise Credential to Sign In to 173 Microsoft 365 Tenants
item.description:
A compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup credential was used to authenticate into 173 Microsoft 365 tenants in under two and a half hours, with one tenant showing Global Administrator privilege escalation and backdoored trusted apps.
Key findings:
- On October 15 between 06:13 and 08:34 UTC, a threat actor used a stolen credential for ConnectWise Cloud Backup (app ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae) to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens across 173 partner and customer tenants, authenticating from 144.172.64[.]128. The actor traversed tenants in sorted GUID order seconds apart, consistent with automated scripting against a prebuilt target list. The same IP conducted password spraying against four law firm tenants on October 13 and 14.
- Because ConnectWise Cloud Backup holds broad pre-consented permissions, the attacker inherited read/write access to mailboxes via Exchange Web Services, OneDrive, SharePoint files, Teams chats, and directory data without needing to compromise any individual user. Revoking user sessions does not stop this. Tokens already issued remain valid up to 90 minutes even after the app is disabled.
- In at least one tenant, the ConnectWise Cloud Management app for Microsoft Teams (app ID 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640) assigned itself Global Administrator, then ran a Python script (User-Agent: Python-urllib/3.12) that added new client secrets to an MSP management application and a security platform application. Adding secrets to an MSP management app extends potential access to every customer tenant that app is consented into.
- Critically, some of this access, specifically directory reads through Microsoft Graph, leaves no audit trail. Scope of data exposure cannot be fully reconstructed from logs alone, which makes waiting for evidence of access the wrong posture here.
- ConnectWise has closed Cloud Backup application access until further notice and found no evidence backup data itself was exfiltrated, but the credential compromise and downstream privilege escalation represent a live and expanding blast radius for any MSP with the app installed.
Practitioner takeaway: Go to Microsoft Entra Admin Center, Monitoring, Sign-in logs, and select the Service principal sign-ins tab, not the default user tab. Filter by application ID 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae and look for authentication from 144.172.64[.]128 or any non-Azure, non-IPv6 source. Then pull Entra audit logs and hunt for any ConnectWise or SkyKick application adding itself to a directory role, and audit all app registrations for new client secrets created since October 13. Enable Microsoft Graph activity logs if not already on. Disable the app in every tenant until ConnectWise confirms full credential rotation.

item.title: The First Four-Digit Patch Tuesday. Only One Flaw is Under Attack.
item.description:
October 2026 Patch Tuesday hits 1,418 Microsoft CVEs, the first four-digit release, with 36 CVEs confirmed exploited across all vendors, 35 of them outside Microsoft. One Microsoft zero-day is under active attack; the real fire is at the network edge.
- CVE-2026-96951, the only Microsoft CVE under active exploitation this month, is a Windows Shell Mark-of-the-Web bypass, CVSS 8.8, with functional exploit code confirmed in the CVRF temporal vector. CISA KEV deadline was 16 October. MOTW is what triggers Protected View, SmartScreen, and macro-blocking for internet-sourced files; this flaw strips that tag entirely, so a crafted file delivered by email or chat opens as if the user created it locally. The artifact to hunt: files written by browsers or mail clients that are missing the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream. Deploy to user endpoints first, not servers, because delivery is social and the target is a person. Do not treat Protected View or SmartScreen as compensating controls while this is unpatched.
- The Ivanti Connect Secure chain (CVE-2026-104935, CVSS 8.6, KEV added 13 October, deadline 16 October) is only half-closed. Volexity documented UTA0576 exploiting three flaws: an auth bypass in welcome.cgi, a file-write race in wu.cgi where an uploaded script executes before validation deletes it, and a privilege escalation in the dsinvoked broker that carries no CVE and has no patch, with Ivanti saying a fix is coming "in the coming weeks." Exploitation began 3 October against a fully patched appliance. Ivanti's Integrity Checker may not detect this: memory and network forensics are required. Volexity's indicators include IP 108.165.147[.]64, files under /data/.icscap/ and /tmp/, and high volumes of welcome.cgi requests with mismatched X-DSCGI-PATH headers. Volexity assessed with medium confidence that UTA0576 is using LLMs for exploit development and post-exploitation.
- Citrix NetScaler contributed three exploited CVEs across two waves. CVE-2026-88771 (CVSS 9.5, unauthenticated command execution, every ADC and Gateway in default config) and CVE-2026-88772 (9.5, memory overflow via DTLS) hit 27 September, with Kevin Beaumont observing webshells dropped since early September, weeks before disclosure. Wave two brought CVE-2026-88779 (8.7) in the SAML implementation on 4 October. Anyone who patched wave one must patch again for SAML. Critically: patching does not remove existing backdoors. Take a forensic snapshot before upgrading and check for /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.ctxs.receiver, the NX-CVE-OK marker, and php_flag engine on in httpd.conf.
- Check Point standard LivePatch does not fix CVE-2026-93616 (CVSS 9.8, pre-auth path traversal in Security Management, Multi-Domain, Log Server and SmartEvent): the named Jumbo or Security Hotfix from sk1000171 must be applied. Exploitation of CVE-2026-93616 began 23 July, two months before the fix shipped. CVE-2026-85102 (9.8, certificate validation bypass on gateways running VPN) was under attack three days after its patch released. F5 CVE-2026-94127 (9.8, heap overflow in BIG-IP APM OAuth) is reachable where a virtual server has both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile; detection is behavioral: repeated invalid-token UserInfo failures from one source in /var/log/apm, or TMM crashes.
- On 8 October, CISA added five legacy CVEs simultaneously as part of joint advisory AA26-281A, attributed to Chinese 🇨🇳 government-linked actors enabled by Integrity Technology Group: ProFTPD CVE-2015-3306 (EPSS 0.995), ISC BIND CVE-2015-5477 (0.994), Apache Struts CVE-2016-3081 (0.961), ONLYOFFICE CVE-2021-3199, and Strapi CVE-2023-22894. The tradecraft includes a custom scanner called MicroScan, password spraying against Exchange, renamed SoftEther VPN clients for persistence, DCSync, and a PHP bot that collects and uploads email. The remediation deadline was three days from publication.
Practitioner takeaway: Inventory DNS servers that are co-resident with Active Directory before scheduling the patch window for CVE-2026-83869 (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated RCE, no interaction), because code execution in the DNS service on a domain controller is a direct path to domain compromise. For the Ivanti chain, hunt /data/.icscap/ and /tmp/ for unexpected files, review welcome.cgi logs for X-DSCGI-PATH header mismatches, and treat the dsinvoked broker escalation as unpatched regardless of your current version. The full IOC set and 72-hour remediation plan are in the OPSWAT report.

CVE-2026-88771 (CVSS 9.5, unauthenticated command execution, every ADC and Gateway in default config) and CVE-2026-88772 (9.5, memory overflow via DTLS) hit 27 September, with Kevin Beaumont observing webshells dropped since early September, weeks before disclosure. Wave two brought CVE-2026-88779 (8.7) in the SAML implementation on 4 October. Anyone who patched wave one must patch again for SAML. Critically: patching does not remove existing backdoors. Take a forensic snapshot before upgrading and check for /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/custom/.ctxs.receiver, the NX-CVE-OK marker, and php_flag engine on in httpd.conf.

- Check Point standard LivePatch does not fix CVE-2026-93616 (CVSS 9.8, pre-auth path traversal in Security Management, Multi-Domain, Log Server and SmartEvent): the named Jumbo or Security Hotfix from sk1000171 must be applied. Exploitation of CVE-2026-93616 began 23 July, two months before the fix shipped. CVE-2026-85102 (9.8, certificate validation bypass on gateways running VPN) was under attack three days after its patch released. F5 CVE-2026-94127 (9.8, heap overflow in BIG-IP APM OAuth) is reachable where a virtual server has both an APM access policy and an OAuth profile; detection is behavioral: repeated invalid-token UserInfo failures from one source in /var/log/apm, or TMM crashes.

- On 8 October, CISA added five legacy CVEs simultaneously as part of joint advisory AA26-281A, attributed to Chinese 🇨🇳 government-linked actors enabled by Integrity Technology Group: ProFTPD CVE-2015-3306 (EPSS 0.995), ISC BIND CVE-2015-5477 (0.994), Apache Struts CVE-2016-3081 (0.961), ONLYOFFICE CVE-2021-3199, and Strapi CVE-2023-22894. The tradecraft includes a custom scanner called MicroScan, password spraying against Exchange, renamed SoftEther VPN clients for persistence, DCSync, and a PHP bot that collects and uploads email. The remediation deadline was three days from publication.

Practitioner takeaway: Inventory DNS servers that are co-resident with Active Directory before scheduling the patch window for CVE-2026-83869 (CVSS 9.8, unauthenticated RCE, no interaction), because code execution in the DNS service on a domain controller is a direct path to domain compromise. For the Ivanti chain, hunt /data/.icscap/ and /tmp/ for unexpected files, review welcome.cgi logs for X-DSCGI-PATH header mismatches, and treat the dsinvoked broker escalation as unpatched regardless of your current version. The full IOC set and 72-hour remediation plan are in the OPSWAT report.

item.title: AdFection: Beyond the Click: Citizen Lab Exposes Ad-Delivered Spyware Networks
item.description:
Citizen Lab exposes Israeli 🇮🇱 spyware vendor Candiru using ad-bidding infrastructure to deliver zero-click exploits at scale, confirmed against Al Jazeera with at least 45 devices targeted across 2024-2025.
Key findings:
- Discover-Tech's MyDSP platform bid on nearly 3.77 billion ad impressions across March-June 2026, winning roughly 442 million, appearing across 120,000+ websites and 70,000+ mobile apps. The database Citizen Lab reviewed showed three advertisers with nine advertiser-domain combinations. This is not theoretical reach: the scale gave operators a surveillance dragnet capable of fingerprinting devices before any exploit is deployed.
- The attack model is called AdFection. No user click is required. When an ad loads, the code behind it can collect advertising identifiers, IP addresses, and browser characteristics to profile the device. Operators then use that telemetry to select high-value targets for follow-on exploitation. The profiling and the delivery are baked into the same ad-bidding workflow that ordinary browsing depends on.
- Al Jazeera supplied Citizen Lab with network logs that confirmed the activity. Researchers linked zero-click attacks in 2024 and 2025 to Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech advertisements, with at least 45 devices inside the broadcaster targeted. Candiru, placed on the US 🇺🇸 Entity List in 2021, has since operated under the name Integrity Labs. Citizen Lab also identified infrastructure links to surveillance companies Bindecy and Intelos, suggesting Discover-Tech served multiple spyware customers.
- Advertising impressions appeared on networks associated with the Pentagon, NATO, the United Nations, the European Commission, and the International Criminal Court. This does not confirm infection at those organizations, but it shows the infrastructure reached devices inside sensitive environments where device activity has direct intelligence value. Government, defense, media, and critical-infrastructure networks across multiple countries appeared in the bidding records.
- Discover-Tech held approved-vendor status with Google and IAB Europe for years before this investigation. Following Citizen Lab's findings, Google terminated its access to advertising exchanges, IAB Europe suspended its vendor status, and Beeswax, Eskimi, and Vungle/Liftoff took separate blocking or review actions. The fact that the company passed routine vetting for this long illustrates why automated scanning of advertising partners is insufficient: targeting rules that serve different code to different users are invisible to most platform-level checks.
Practitioner takeaway: Review network traffic generated at ad-load time on devices used by executives, journalists, and staff with access to sensitive systems. Look for unexpected outbound connections or script fetches that occur without any user interaction when a page or app loads an advertisement. Al Jazeera's network logs were the artifact that made attribution possible here: organizations should ensure that DNS query logs, proxy logs, and endpoint network telemetry are retained with enough fidelity to reconstruct what code ran when an ad loaded. NSA and CISA have both recommended ad-blocking software for government and organizational use since 2018 and 2020 respectively. For high-risk device populations, enforce ad and tracker blocking at the network gateway and disable ad personalization on managed devices. The full Citizen Lab report contains the technical evidence supporting the Al Jazeera attribution.

item.title: China-Linked Hackers Exploited BeyondTrust Zero-Day to Take Over Remote Support Servers
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage group Armory Castle exploited CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS 9.3) in BeyondTrust Remote Support as a zero-day, deploying the SAWFLY web shell and BARECLAW SOCKS5 tunneler to steal credentials and pivot into downstream enterprise systems.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102764 is an improper origin validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support's internal messaging component (versions 24.3.1 through 26.2.3). Exploitation was first observed August 29, 2026, on a single self-hosted appliance. This was a targeted zero-day hit, not a spray campaign. Armory Castle's documented pattern is selective early exploitation, then broad opportunistic exploitation once a flaw goes public. SaaS customers were patched October 9; self-hosted customers need the BT26-05-RS patch manually applied.
- Post-exploitation was surgical and showed deep appliance knowledge. The actor copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, set SUID and root ownership to establish a persistent privilege escalation backdoor that survives reboots. They then used BeyondTrust's own proprietary /ns/sbin/bt-secrets CLI utility to harvest stored passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials directly from the appliance's secrets management database, and abused configuration templates to gain passwordless root to the site service account.
- Lateral movement used the appliance's own functionality as a weapon. Armory Castle pivoted through compromised administrator credentials into the Remote Support application itself, launched remote sessions to downstream endpoints via the appliance's Jump Item list, and obtained full file-system access to internal systems to exfiltrate documents. BARECLAW, a custom C-based SOCKS5 proxy tunneler, relayed TCP traffic outbound, with persistence enforced by modifying /ns/config/haproxy.conf to expose BARECLAW directly from the internet.
- Detection was actively suppressed. The actor systematically deleted system, web server, and application-level logs throughout the intrusion. Network traffic was blended using commercial VPN exit nodes and compromised SOHO routers. Mandiant's researchers note SAWFLY provided bidirectional encrypted C2 via a lightweight PHP web shell for interactive access throughout.
- Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221 or Warp Panda) has been active since October 2023 with a consistent playbook against network edge appliances: Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2023-4966), Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2025-0282). Targets span legal services, SaaS providers, BPOs, technology, and government. BeyondTrust's own assessment notes the group maintains ongoing AI-assisted exploit chain development against pre-selected high-value products.
Practitioner takeaway: Any internet-exposed BeyondTrust Remote Support appliance running a vulnerable version during the August 29 to October 9 window should be treated as compromised until reviewed. Start with file integrity checks for /usr/bin/dbus-authd (SUID shell copy) and changes to /ns/config/haproxy.conf. Audit bt-secrets CLI invocation history for unauthorized credential access. Review Jump Item session logs for lateral movement to downstream systems, and check for the SAWFLY PHP web shell on the appliance's web root. Log deletion means absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: pull any surviving OS-level audit records, network flow data, and upstream firewall logs to reconstruct the timeline.

item.title: CVE-2026-88771: Inside the Exploitation of a Critical NetScaler RCE Vulnerability
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771, a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated RCE in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway, is actively exploited in the wild and listed in CISA KEV. Patch immediately, but preserve forensics first.
- CVE-2026-88771 requires no authentication and no optional features. The attack works by poisoning the HTTP access log with Base64-encoded shell commands in a User-Agent value beginning "INDEX:", then submitting a forged pitboss PPE failure string to /nf/auth/doAuthentication.do or /cgi/login. The legitimate NetScaler Perl script /netscaler/ns_monuploadd_err.pl later processes PPE failure records from /var/log/ns.log, selects the last matching line, and passes attacker-controlled content to a shell without escaping metacharacters. That is the trigger: no direct exploit request fires the code, a trusted diagnostic script does it.
- Once execution lands, the payload creates directories, writes fingerprint HTML files using the prefix Nx_ (observed as Nx_7508.html and Nx_5936.html) across /var/vpn/bookmark/, /netscaler/ns_gui/vpn/, /var/netscaler/gui/vpn/, /var/vpn/theme/, and /var/netscaler/logon/LogonPoint/, then drops PHP and Perl web shells with the same naming pattern. It also modifies /etc/httpd.conf to flip php_engine off to php_engine on and appends AddHandler cgi-script .pl, then sends Apache a HUP signal. An inline variant fetched a Rust-based FreeBSD x64 binary named kw2-freebsd-x64-s11 from 209.141.43[.]95 to /var/kw2s11 and executed it.
- ThreatLabz observed a coordinated burst from at least 26 source IP addresses over roughly six to seven minutes, all following the same log-poisoning and FreeBSD payload-delivery sequence. The download server at 209.141.43[.]95 also appeared in exploitation of CVE-2026-75650 (StyleSmuggler, CVSS 10.0, Adobe Commerce and Magento). Shared infrastructure across two unrelated platforms suggests a common operator or malware-distribution service, though attribution is not confirmed. The full IOC table with 27 source IPs is in the report.
- CISA warns that patching before evidence collection can destroy forensic visibility. Before upgrading, capture a VM snapshot where possible, collect the NetScaler technical support bundle, remote syslog data, and packet-engine core dumps. Then search HTTP access logs for User-Agent values starting with "INDEX:" followed by Base64 content. Search /var/log/ns.log and /var/log/messages for forged pitboss PPE strings containing shell syntax. Find newly written files in webroot paths with: find /netscaler/ns_gui/ /var/netscaler/gui/ /var/vpn/ -type f -mtime -3. Look for Nx_*.php and Nx_*.pl alongside unexpected Nx_*.html fingerprint files. Check /etc/httpd.conf for php_engine on and AddHandler cgi-script .pl modifications. Run ps aux and grep for shells spawned under the nobody service context, and netstat -an to surface unexpected listening ports.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for the INDEX: User-Agent pattern in HTTP access logs and forged pitboss PPE strings in ns.log before you touch the upgrade. Those two log sources together reconstruct the full pre-execution chain. Fixed builds are NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1-73.46 and 13.1-64.29. Rotate all credentials, tokens, and certificates stored on or reachable through any appliance confirmed compromised.
